records.name: Adaptive immune resistance
records.tldr: An immune attack can induce its own restraint: signals from responding T cells raise inhibitory proteins on nearby cells. This induced defence differs from resistance acquired after a treatment response.
records.summary:
The sequence proposed by Taube and colleagues and mapped in more detail since is a loop. A T cell recognises a tumour peptide on HLA and releases interferon gamma; the interferon acts through the Janus kinases JAK1 and JAK2 in nearby tumour and immune cells; PD-L1 rises; PD-L1 binds PD-1 on the T cell and damps it. In melanoma cell lines, Garcia-Diaz and colleagues found that the interferon gamma, JAK1 and JAK2, STAT1, STAT2 and STAT3, IRF1 axis primarily regulates PD-L1, with IRF1 binding the PD-L1 promoter, and biopsies from patients with melanoma showed enrichment of that interferon signature and of STAT and IRF1 target genes in tumours that responded to anti-PD-1 treatment.

PD-L1 is not the only brake that follows the attack. Spranger and colleagues found in human melanoma that the T-cell-inflamed tumours were the ones with high indoleamine 2,3-dioxygenase (IDO), PD-L1 and regulatory T cells, and in mice that all three depended on CD8 T cells being present: IDO and PD-L1 through interferon gamma, and regulatory T cells through CCR4-binding chemokines with some induced proliferation. Their reading was that these pathways are driven by the immune response rather than orchestrated by the cancer cells.

Evidence from tissue. In human melanocytic lesions, 98% of PD-L1-positive (B7-H1-positive) tumours had tumour-infiltrating lymphocytes compared with 28% of PD-L1-negative tumours; positive melanocytes sat almost always immediately next to lymphocytes, and interferon gamma was detected at the interface but not in PD-L1-negative tumours (Taube and colleagues). The same colocalisation appeared in inflamed benign naevi, which fits PD-L1 as a response to tissue inflammation. In triple-negative breast cancer, Gruosso and colleagues described an immunoreactive group whose tumours had granzyme B-positive CD8 T cells inside cancer-cell regions, a type 1 interferon signature and elevated IDO and PD-L1, the pattern adaptive resistance predicts; that is an association in tissue and not a direct test of the loop. The alternative, called innate or constitutive resistance, is PD-L1 driven by the cancer cell's own signalling regardless of T cells.

A functionally important loss of JAK1 or JAK2 can impair the tumour cell response to interferon gamma. In four people with metastatic melanoma that relapsed on anti-PD-1 treatment, two relapse samples carried loss-of-function JAK1 or JAK2 mutations with deletion of the remaining normal allele, and truncating JAK1 or JAK2 mutations left the cells unresponsive to interferon gamma (Zaretsky and colleagues). The JAK2-deficient relapse cells lost interferon-gamma-induced PD-L1 and class-I increases but retained responses to interferon alfa and beta. In engineered melanoma cells, JAK1 or JAK2 loss did not abolish recognition by the tested NY-ESO-1-specific T cells. Loss of inducibility is therefore different from absence of all baseline recognition. This selected series does not estimate a frequency for all cancers.

notes: Reading the label. PD-L1-positive does not mean the tumour is suppressing the immune system on its own, because in adaptive resistance the signal is a reaction to T cells. PD-L1-negative does not mean no immune attack: staining is patchy, assays differ and other brakes exist. Adaptive resistance also differs from acquired resistance, which means a tumour that responded to treatment and then stopped responding; here 'adaptive' names an induced defence, and the two can overlap without being the same thing.

A PD-L1 stain measures protein on defined tumour and immune cells, not why it is present. Colocalization with lymphocytes and interferon-related expression can support induced expression, while a uniform lymphocyte-poor pattern raises other hypotheses; neither pattern proves a cause. Adding interferon gamma and measuring PD-L1 tests inducibility in a laboratory model. Appropriate pathway perturbations and controls investigate causation, and neither that assay nor a tissue score measures the entire in-vivo feedback loop or treatment benefit.

In a fictional biopsy, PD-L1 is found at a lymphocyte-rich border but not at the centre. That distribution is consistent with induced expression; it does not prove the proposed loop. A negative region does not establish absence of immune attack elsewhere, and other inhibitory pathways may operate. A positive PD-L1 result alone also cannot distinguish induced from constitutive expression.

What the loop means for treatment is a hypothesis to test. PD-1 and PD-L1 drugs interrupt the last step, the binding of PD-L1 to PD-1. Spranger and colleagues argued that checkpoint approaches might be preferentially beneficial for patients with a pre-existing T-cell-inflamed microenvironment, which is a reading of their data and not a trial result.

records.name: Adenosine and IDO: two separate routes that can restrain immune responses
records.tldr: Adenosine can signal immune cells to reduce activity; the IDO1 enzyme starts a separate route that breaks down tryptophan, an amino acid. Finding their components in a tumour does not prove immune suppression or drug benefit. An IDO1 blocker added to pembrolizumab did not improve melanoma outcomes in a phase 3 trial.
records.summary: The adenosine route works outside cells. CD39 (ENTPD1) and CD73 (NT5E) are enzymes that help generate adenosine from extracellular ATP and ADP, and adenosine then acts on cell-surface receptors, including the A2A receptor on T cells. The enzymes can sit on immune cells, cancer cells or other tissue cells, so the source has to be measured and not assumed. The IDO route works inside a producing cell: IDO1 starts the breakdown of tryptophan along the kynurenine pathway. IDO is not an adenosine receptor and does not degrade ATP, so the two routes should not be merged into one 'suppressive axis'.

notes: The mechanism evidence is mostly from mice and cell experiments. CD39 and CD73 distinguished regulatory T cells from other T cells, and regulatory T cells from Cd39-null mice had impaired suppression in vitro and failed to block allograft rejection in vivo (Deaglio et al., 2007). Deleting the A2A receptor in the host led to rejection of established immunogenic tumours in about 60 per cent of A2A-deficient mice, with none rejected in normal mice (Ohta et al., 2006). The same mouse study reported autoimmunity during melanoma rejection in the A2A-deficient mice and proposed that the receptor in T cells also helps prevent autoimmune tissue damage, so a pathway that restrains antitumour T cells may also protect normal tissue, and any assessment of an inhibitor has to weigh that trade-off. A subset of plasmacytoid dendritic cells in mouse tumour-draining lymph nodes expressed immunosuppressive levels of IDO and suppressed T-cell responses, and anergy was prevented by disrupting the IDO gene or by an IDO inhibitor (Munn et al., 2004). The same paper reported, as a separate observation in the human samples studied, that IDO-expressing cells in tumour-draining lymph nodes correlated with a worse clinical outcome; that is an association, and the authors noted the human cells' relationship to the mouse subset was still to be determined.

The layers of evidence are different and should be kept apart: a protein or RNA signal shows a component is present, a biochemical assay shows enzyme activity or metabolite, a functional experiment shows an immune effect, and a trial shows whether blocking it helps patients. A blood adenosine result is sensitive to handling: adenosine has a half-life of 1 to 2 seconds in human blood at 37 degrees Celsius, and in a sampling experiment recovery of labelled adenosine was 89 per cent with an inhibitor mix delivered at the catheter tip but 7 per cent when the mix was added only after the catheter (Shryock et al., 1990), and even a well-handled blood level does not locate the producing cells. No single expression cutoff for CD39, CD73 or IDO1 is validated in the sources cited here to choose an inhibitor, so a report should state the sample site, timing and units and not rely on one threshold. The clinical test of the IDO1 route was negative for that regimen: in ECHO-301/KEYNOTE-252, 706 people with unresectable or metastatic melanoma not previously treated with a PD-1 or PD-L1 blocker received pembrolizumab with epacadostat or with placebo, and median progression-free survival was 4.7 against 4.9 months (hazard ratio 1.00, 95 per cent confidence interval 0.83 to 1.21), with overall survival hazard ratio 1.13 (0.86 to 1.49) (Long et al., 2019). The authors wrote that the usefulness of IDO1 inhibition to enhance anti-PD-1 therapy remains uncertain. That bounds one drug, one dose and one disease; it neither proves all IDO research futile nor validates another inhibitor or cancer. By the same logic, a tumour section that stains for both CD73 and IDO1 shows two measured proteins in the sampled cells: it does not show one dominant suppressive mechanism or the best inhibitor, because each route still needs its own activity and functional question.

records.name: T-cell anergy
records.tldr: A living T cell can remain less responsive after an antigen encounter. A weak test result alone does not establish anergy.
records.summary:
Anergy is antigen-related reduced responsiveness that persists into a later controlled response test. In Jenkins and Schwartz's mouse and T-cell-clone experiments, chemically altered presenting cells induced reduced responsiveness to subsequent antigen stimulation with normal presenting cells. Macian and colleagues identified an NFAT-associated anergy gene programme in mechanistic experiments. These findings are model evidence, not a universal tumour-cell classifier.

Exhaustion is a distinct differentiation programme associated with persistent stimulation. Anergy, exhaustion, external suppression, absent antigen-specific cells and assay failure are different possible explanations for a low response. Low interleukin-2 alone leaves the mechanism unresolved. Check specificity, viable-cell recovery, stimulus controls, responsive comparators and response history; measure division and cytokine responses under matched conditions. Laboratory rescue does not establish tumour recognition, safe killing or clinical benefit.

notes: Anergy is persistent reduced antigen-driven responsiveness after a defined antigen encounter, assessed with a suitable later challenge. It is not simply resting, a naive identity, missing support at one encounter or failure to divide now. Altered-presenting-cell induction followed by normal-presenting-cell retesting in mouse clones supports this distinction.

In defined mechanistic experiments, unbalanced calcium signalling and NFAT without cooperative AP-1 promoted an anergy-associated gene programme. Reduced IL-2, a response-supporting cytokine, can accompany anergy. Signal strength, inhibitory context and experimental definition matter; inadequate costimulation is an example rather than a universal diagnosis.

Low IL-2 or a negative ELISpot response alone does not establish anergy. Confirm antigen-specific cells, viable-cell recovery, matched stimulus and responsive comparators, response history and relevant pathway perturbations. Report dividing-cell fractions or cytokine concentration with assay units and conditions. Missing recognition, damaged preparations, suppression or exhaustion remain alternatives.

Anergy can contribute to tolerance of mature immune cells. Protective restraint and tumour immune escape can overlap; changing a laboratory response does not establish restored specificity, tumour access, safe killing or clinical benefit.

Anergy and exhaustion are distinct programmes, not compulsory successive stages or interchangeable labels for dysfunction. Dysfunction is a broader description that may also include senescence, external suppression and missing recognition. Classic clonal anergy often limits growth and IL-2 while retaining effector functions and can respond to added IL-2; adaptive tolerance has broader deficits and can reverse after antigen removal. These distinctions come from model and review evidence, not clinical cutoffs.

Fictional independent populations A and B share verified specificity and suitable later stimulation. A has altered initial support followed by a controlled persistent defect; B has persistent stimulation with several functional deficits and compatible programme evidence. These support anergy-compatible and exhaustion-compatible explanations respectively. C with only low IL-2 remains unassigned. Viability, specificity and positive controls are necessary; no one control establishes state and no A-to-B transition or checkpoint-rescue prediction follows.

records.name: Antibody
records.tldr: A typical IgG antibody has antigen-binding arms and a stem that can interact with other parts of the immune system. Binding alone does not specify its function.
records.summary: A typical IgG has two antigen-binding arms; receptor binding and cross-reactivity depend on the particular molecule and test system, while its stem (the Fc region) can recruit immune cells and complement or extend the antibody's life in the blood. Therapeutic antibodies block growth receptors (trastuzumab on HER2, cetuximab on EGFR), release the brakes on T cells (pembrolizumab on PD-1), flag cancer cells for immune killing (rituximab on CD20), or serve as the targeting vehicle of ADCs and radioimmunotherapy. Bispecific formats have two binding specificities. Some are designed to bring a T cell and a target cell together; their structures and functions vary. Fab, the arm with the binding site, and Fc, the stem, are separate parts: binding does not guarantee killing, and Fc effector contacts need compatible effector cells or complement. Antibodies that bind the same target can act differently: a blocking antibody, an antibody-drug conjugate and a bispecific format can share a target and still differ in what follows.

records.name: Antigen
records.tldr: An antigen is a molecular target an immune receptor can recognise. Recognition alone does not establish immune activation or safe tumour targeting.
records.summary: Most cancer antigens are ordinary human proteins that a tumour makes in unusual amounts (HER2, TROP2, CD19, PSMA), so drugs targeting them also touch normal cells that carry a little; truly tumour-specific antigens arise from mutations (neoantigens) or from viral proteins. A good drug antigen is abundant on tumour cells, scarce on essential normal tissue, and stable over time. Tumours escape by losing the antigen, which is how CD19-negative relapse defeats CAR-T, and by hiding the pieces of antigen they would normally display to T cells. Recognition differs from immunogenicity, the ability to elicit an immune response in a particular setting. An antibody can recognise an accessible part of a molecule directly, whereas a conventional peptide-directed T-cell receptor recognises a processed peptide together with a particular HLA molecule, so a surface-expression result cannot by itself establish peptide-HLA display. A self molecule can be an antigen, and tumour-associated is not the same as tumour-specific.

records.name: Antigen-processing machinery (APM)
records.tldr: Cells cut up proteins, move some fragments to a loading site and place them on display molecules that T cells can inspect. Having a protein inside a cell does not guarantee its fragment is shown.
records.summary:
Antigen-processing machinery (APM) is the set of proteins that generate, transport and load peptides onto HLA. A common class I route has five steps. (1) The proteasome cuts intracellular proteins into fragments, which can create a useful peptide or destroy it. (2) The transporter associated with antigen processing, TAP1 with TAP2, moves peptides into the endoplasmic reticulum; Shepherd et al. (1993) showed in a cell-free system that TAP1 is part of an ATP-dependent, sequence-selective peptide translocator. (3) ERAP1 and ERAP2 trim amino acids from the front end. York et al. (2002) found that ERAP1 can enhance or limit presentation by trimming epitopes to 8 to 9 residues, and Saveanu et al. (2005) found complementary human ERAP1 and ERAP2 activity, so more expression does not universally improve display. A class I HLA heavy chain assembles with beta-2 microglobulin (B2M) and a peptide, with helpers such as tapasin. (4) Stable peptide-HLA complexes reach the surface; the peptide stays held by HLA. (5) A compatible T-cell receptor on a conventional CD8 T cell may recognise the pair; recognition is a separate gate and display alone does not show killing.

Class II HLA commonly loads peptides in vesicles that process acquired proteins. An invariant chain protects the new groove and directs it there; after cutting, a remaining fragment is exchanged for other peptides with help from HLA-DM, and conventional CD4 T cells inspect these displays. Cross-presentation lets externally acquired material reach class I. The scheme is a common route, not a rule for every peptide.

A cancer cell may keep an altered protein and still show little of its peptide, and a shared processing defect can affect several targets at once, so adding candidate peptides does not bypass the bottleneck. Low expression, gene loss and a functional defect are different findings: a weak RNA signal does not prove deletion. Interferon gamma can increase presentation machinery when its signalling pathway and the required genes are intact, and cannot replace a deleted B2M or HLA gene. Sucker et al. (2017) described melanoma lesions in which JAK1 or JAK2 defects gave interferon-gamma resistance and evolved into HLA class I negative, T-cell-resistant lesions with antigen-presentation genes silenced and no longer inducible. Zaretsky et al. (2016) found, in biopsies from patients with acquired resistance to PD-1 blockade, JAK1 or JAK2 loss of function in two of four patients and a truncating B2M mutation with lost surface class I in a third. These are melanoma observations, not treatment-benefit evidence.

Evidence layers differ. DNA sequence and copy number show gene retention or alteration but not expression or function; RNA shows sampled gene activity but not protein, assembly or display; protein staining or flow cytometry detects protein but not which peptide is shown; HLA-associated peptide recovery shows a peptide was recovered with HLA in that preparation but not its cell of origin or recognition; controlled T-cell recognition shows function against tested targets. Peptide loading can bypass processing, so rescue by supplied peptide supports a bottleneck under those conditions only. Binding prediction is not presentation, and CD4 help is not proof of CD8 tumour recognition.

In the 14-participant TNBC-MERIT vaccine study, one recurrent tumour had downregulated antigen-presentation transcripts, including B2M, and nearly complete class-I protein loss compared with the earlier specimen. Sahin and colleagues considered B2M downregulation the most probable driver. This was an expression and protein observation in that recurrence, not a demonstrated new B2M DNA mutation, a recurrence probability or proof of a rescue treatment. Allele loss, RNA downregulation and a shared class-I assembly defect require different evidence; adding more source windows does not itself repair the failed step.

The common proteasome-TAP route is not a rule for every class-I peptide. A TAP or proteasome-component alteration, reduced RNA or one weak stain does not by itself establish complete loss of every class-I display; establish the functional defect and its scope. B2M-dependent assembly, loss of a restricting HLA allele and an inducible signalling defect are different dependencies. The accessible Roche and Cresswell review supports the specified common processing and class-II exchange steps; it does not turn the unread Bookshelf chapters into verified sources.

records.name: Apoptosis
records.tldr: Apoptosis is a regulated process that dismantles a cell. Whether the dying cell stimulates protective immunity is a separate question.
records.summary: The mitochondrial route uses BCL-2-family control of BAX and BAK and cytochrome c release. In cell experiments, combined BAX and BAK loss blocked mitochondrial responses to several apoptotic stimuli; this does not establish resistance to all forms of death. Death-receptor signals provide another route. Apoptosis is not inherently immune-silent: anthracycline-treated tumour cells showed calreticulin-dependent immunogenicity in mouse experiments. A death marker, a mitochondrial response and sustained killing answer different questions. Protein abundance alone cannot establish dependence or choose a treatment.

notes: Intrinsic apoptosis involves mitochondrial outer-membrane permeabilisation, cytochrome c release into the cytosol, apoptosome assembly and caspase-9 activation upstream of executioner caspases such as caspase-3 and caspase-7. Death-receptor signalling can activate caspase-8; BID cleavage links this route to mitochondria. Initiator and executioner roles differ.

The BCL-2 family contains survival proteins, including BCL-2, BCL-XL and MCL-1; BH3-only stress mediators, including BIM, BID and PUMA; and pore-forming effectors BAX and BAK. In experimental cells, loss of both BAX and BAK blocked several mitochondrial apoptotic responses, rather than every possible form of death.

Cytochrome c moves from the mitochondrial intermembrane compartment, including crista stores, across the outer membrane to the cytosol. It does not begin in the matrix. The inner membrane separates these compartments; the spatial sketch is simplified, with no implied pore stoichiometry.

A stain for BCL-XL measures abundance rather than survival dependence. BCL2 and BCL2L1 are different genes, and inhibitor selectivity matters. Souers and colleagues re-engineered dual BCL-2/BCL-XL inhibition into BCL-2-selective ABT-199, sparing human platelets; early tumour lysis in three refractory chronic lymphocytic leukaemia patients does not establish benefit in every tumour. A mitochondrial response, caspase marker, sustained killing and immune protection remain separate outcomes. Keep cell identity, timing, handling controls and later survival or regrowth with cleaved-caspase assays, membrane readouts and microscopy. Mitochondrial BH3 challenges test readiness under a defined protocol, rather than completed killing or clinical benefit.

Compare mechanism, morphology, immune consequence and living arrest separately. Apoptosis uses regulated dismantling; necrotic morphology describes boundary failure; ferroptosis requires iron-dependent lipid damage causing death; immunogenicity requires a compatible adaptive response; senescence is a living arrest. These categories are not mutually exclusive outcomes or a universal appearance-based classifier.

In the fictional killing experiment, rescue by both an iron chelator and a lipid-protecting compound with no caspase-inhibitor rescue supports a ferroptosis hypothesis. Check lipid damage, death timing, perturbation specificity and GPX4 or glutathione-related mechanisms before attribution; immunogenicity is a separate test. A single stain is not enough.

records.name: Bulk RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) and the full transcriptome
records.tldr: Bulk RNA sequencing measures captured messages pooled across a tissue sample, including contributions from multiple cell types.
records.summary: RNA carries cellular messages; bulk sequencing samples those messages from combined tissue after protocol-specific capture and preparation. Analysis assigns usable observations to genes or transcripts and applies a defined comparison scale. A change can reflect cell composition, expression within cells or both. Gene totals can conceal transcript differences, and pooled RNA does not directly establish protein localisation, pathway flux or drug dependence.

Name the counting unit and normalisation denominator. Estimated transcript counts, length-adjusted transcripts per million and tagged molecule counts answer different measurement questions. A gene total can conceal splice products; pooled RNA does not directly measure surface protein, pathway flux or drug dependence. Sources: https://salmon.readthedocs.io/en/latest/file_formats.html and https://doi.org/10.1186/s13059-016-0881-8.

Fictional mixture exercise: in two 100-cell samples, increasing identical marker-producing lymphocytes from 20 to 40 doubles their stipulated marker molecules if each contributes one and other cells contribute none. This does not show cancer-cell activation. Equal RNA contribution and matched recovery are assumptions, not measured tissue properties.
Bulk RNA-seq extracts RNA, prepares a library (often cDNA), may select mRNA or deplete rRNA or capture regions; bulk does not mean equal capture of all molecules.
Reads or fragments are assigned to genes or transcripts; shared sequences make assignment ambiguous; a count table is already shaped by preparation and analysis.
A bulk signal can rise because more cells of a type contribute, expression within them rises, or both; deconvolution estimates contributions under a model and does not separate cells.
Gene-level counts can hide isoform differences; a mutant or splice product needs sequence or junction evidence.

Bulk RNA can nominate expressed targets and summarise programmes but does not establish cell origin, surface protein, pathway flux or drug dependence; zero reads is not absence; thousands of genes from one biopsy are not thousands of patients.

Fictional teaching exercise: With equal RNA per cell, a lymphocyte-only marker and 100-cell pieces, raising lymphocytes from 20 to 40 doubles the pooled marker (20 to 40 stipulated molecules) without changing any cancer cell.

Track capture, sequence assignment, read/fragment units, normalisation and transcript calls. Preparation time varies; reference material, process controls and biological replicates test different uncertainties. Degradation, contamination, ambiguous annotation, batch and mixture shifts constrain purpose-specific cutoffs and clinical intended-use validation.

records.name: The cancer-immunity cycle
records.tldr: The cancer-immunity cycle maps linked steps from available tumour antigens to T-cell recognition and killing. It helps locate a question or bottleneck; a result at one step does not establish the whole response.
records.summary:
Chen and Mellman’s 2013 framework describes seven linked steps: release of cancer antigens; their collection and presentation; T-cell priming and activation; trafficking; entry into tumour tissue; recognition of cancer cells; and killing. Further antigen release may support another round. In conventional T-cell recognition, a displayed peptide-HLA complex and a suitable T-cell receptor are separate dependencies.

This is a T-cell-centred organizing model, not a universal route, assay result or treatment-selection algorithm. Steps overlap, priming may occur away from the tumour, and other immune mechanisms require their own account. Checkpoints and local tissue conditions affect several steps. Vaccines aim to generate or expand reactive responses, checkpoint drugs interrupt selected inhibitory signals, and engineered cells provide a recognition system and effectors. Each still needs appropriate targets, access, function and safety evidence.

notes: In a fictional vaccine study, blood cells release a cytokine after added-peptide stimulation. This supports reactivity under that assay’s conditions. Added peptide can bypass natural processing, and the result does not establish entry into the sampled tumour, recognition of naturally presenting cancer cells, useful killing or clinical benefit. Antigen release is not priming, blood expansion is not infiltration, and a return arrow does not demonstrate durable protection.

Use the cycle to name the measured step and the next untested dependency. A proposed bottleneck or complementary pair of mechanisms does not establish a beneficial or safe combination. Increasing a response can also affect healthy tissue; the model does not identify a safe intervention by itself.

For a coding change to supply a conventional T-cell target, its information must be expressed, protein produced and processed into a fragment, that peptide displayed with HLA, and a suitable receptor able to recognise the display. DNA, RNA, protein, recovered displayed peptide and controlled recognition are separate observations. A prediction at one step does not measure all the others. This conventional alpha-beta route does not describe every T cell, antibody or natural killer recognition system.

An immune observation suggests a question ladder: identify the cells and their location; ask whether a proposed peptide is produced and displayed; test recognition against appropriate target and background controls; distinguish tissue entry from useful target-specific function; then seek clinical comparisons for benefit and harm. Poor display, few matching cells, failed tissue access and impaired local function are different proposed failures. A count, supplied-peptide response or plausible pathway alone cannot complete that chain. These are task-dependent interpretation questions, not a mandatory clinical test menu.

In an invented vaccine report, one blood clonotype becomes more frequent, its sequence also appears in sampled tumour, a separately tested cell mixture responds to added peptide, and ctDNA becomes undetectable. These are four observations, not proof that this clone killed the cancer. Link the responding cells to a compatible paired receptor, test natural tumour recognition and target death, and preserve each assay's denominator and detection limit. Surgery, chemotherapy, shedding and sampling can also affect ctDNA. Conversely, an unchanged blood repertoire does not exclude a response in unsampled tissue. Temporal coincidence does not establish the causal contribution of one clone.
records.analogy: A relay helps organize the questions: material must be available, presented, recognized and acted on. Several dependencies can be impaired together, and improving one handoff does not establish completion of the response. The map does not predict which treatment will help an individual.
interventions: Radiation, chemotherapy, viruses and antibody-drug conjugates can cause cancer-cell death. Antigen release alone does not establish immunogenic cell death or a useful T-cell response.
Vaccines and antigen-presenting-cell approaches investigate antigen presentation and priming. The framework locates proposed jobs; it does not establish that a particular intervention completes them.
Vascular, chemokine and stromal interventions investigate trafficking or tissue entry in defined systems. Model-specific findings do not establish a general conversion of excluded tumours.

Receptor-engineered cells and engagers change recognition requirements but still depend on accessible targets and functional cells. Conventional TCR recognition remains peptide-HLA-dependent; checkpoint blockade addresses selected inhibitory signals rather than every step.

records.name: CAR-T cell therapy
records.tldr: CAR-T therapy uses T cells carrying an engineered receptor. Approved products treat selected blood cancers, with product-specific eligibility and safety requirements.
records.summary:
CAR-T cell therapy uses T cells carrying a chimeric antigen receptor to recognize a target. FDA-approved products include CD19- and BCMA-directed CAR-T cells for selected blood cancers, including B-cell leukemias, lymphomas and multiple myeloma. The individual product label defines the treatment setting and eligibility. A common autologous approach collects a person’s T cells, engineers and expands them outside the body, then infuses them back; conditioning and follow-up depend on the protocol.

A common antibody-derived CAR joins an external binding region, a hinge or spacer, a membrane anchor and intracellular signaling domains. The receptor is a protein; its encoding instructions and the living cell carrying it are different objects. Approved products and experimental constructs differ in cell source, receptor, manufacturing and clinical setting. Product labels and trial records define their actual uses; a platform name does not establish eligibility or benefit.

In early work, Gross, Waks and Eshhar joined antibody-variable regions to T-cell receptor components in 1989. Eshhar and colleagues subsequently tested single-chain antibody-binding regions joined to gamma or zeta signaling chains in 1993. These experimental designs helped separate recognition from the signaling machinery attached to it.

FDA-approved examples include tisagenlecleucel, axicabtagene ciloleucel, lisocabtagene maraleucel, brexucabtagene autoleucel, obecabtagene autoleucel, idecabtagene vicleucel and ciltacabtagene autoleucel. Their labeled diseases, treatment settings and eligibility differ; the individual product records retain those distinctions.

notes: Generation labels describe common signaling architectures. First-generation constructs use an activation domain, often CD3 zeta; second-generation designs add one costimulatory region; third-generation designs combine two. Fourth-generation and later labels vary across authors. More domains do not establish better patient outcomes. The full binder, spacer, anchor, signaling arrangement and cell preparation still matter.

CD28 and 4-1BB are borrowed intracellular signaling regions, not separately administered receptors. Kawalekar compared metabolic and memory features in defined human-cell experiments. Ramos co-infused two specified second- and third-generation products in lymphoma; different expansion and persistence did not isolate comparative clinical benefit. Neither study ranks all products by signaling-domain name.

Binding, surface CAR expression, activation, proliferation and completed target-cell killing are distinct readouts. Compare otherwise matched constructs, target-positive and target-negative cells, healthy-tissue targets and unstimulated activity. Hudecek found that particular IgG-derived spacers could support killing in a dish yet impair activity in mouse models through Fc interactions.

A peptide-HLA target is an exception to blanket HLA-independent descriptions. Rafiq tested a WT1 peptide presented by HLA-A*02:01 in cell and mouse models; this was a proof of concept, not evidence that every intracellular protein or every HLA type is addressable by that construct.

A 2024 preprint used a pooled signaling-domain library, repeated stimulation and single-cell sequencing to study how domain arrangement affected T-cell states over time. Its membrane-proximal-domain findings are construct-and-assay observations, not a clinical ranking of domains or a validation of pooled-screen hits as treatments.

FDA initiated boxed-warning changes in 2024 for the risk of T-cell malignancies after the then-approved BCMA- or CD19-directed autologous CAR T-cell products. Its communication calls for lifelong monitoring for secondary malignancies. This is a scoped regulatory warning, not a claim that every type of engineered immune cell has the same risk.

In June 2025, FDA eliminated REMS requirements for the named autologous CAR T-cell products in its notice. Product warnings and safety monitoring continued. The manufacturer postmarketing observational studies with 15-year follow-up described in that notice are different from the lifelong patient-monitoring statement in the earlier safety communication.

A receptor-bearing cell, its genetic instructions and its receptor protein are different objects. For a protein-coding instruction, DNA is transcribed into RNA, and a ribosome translates usable messenger RNA into protein. Delivered messenger RNA starts at the translation step. Folding and transport to the membrane still have to occur before a surface receptor can bind its target. In this schematic sequence, simplified shapes and an arrow from recognition toward a response do not show that every cell expressed the receptor or completed killing.

Kymriah’s product description illustrates why borrowed parts do not identify the whole product. Its CD19-binding region is a murine-derived single-chain antibody fragment, followed by a CD8-derived hinge and transmembrane region and the internal 4-1BB/CD137 and CD3-zeta signalling domains. CD8 here names the origin of structural segments, not a claim that the infused preparation contains only CD8 T cells. The label describes enrichment for T cells and permits other cell populations. Autologous source, domain names and architecture do not transfer Kymriah’s clinical results to another construct.

Suppose two fictional CARs differ only in their hinge: both bind purified antigen, but only one kills antigen-bearing cells. Compare surface expression and the geometry of cell contact before concluding that affinity is the problem. Likewise, DNA-positive cells without killing leave RNA production, receptor folding and trafficking, actual binding and signalling as separate possible failure points. Hudecek’s R11 ROR1 experiments illustrate a product-specific constraint: a long spacer enabled recognition of its membrane-proximal epitope, while changes that reduced Fc-receptor binding improved activity in the tested mice. Longer is not a universal design rule. Treat the transmembrane segment as part of the finished construct: assess assembly, surface expression and interactions rather than presume it is a neutral anchor. Unstimulated signalling and responses to repeated target encounters also need separate assessment.

In a fictional population of 100 cancer cells, 80 display target X and 20 do not. Killing the X-positive 80 leaves 20 survivors; ten times as many effector cells does not create X on them. For two targets, suppose 20 cells carry both X and Y, 60 carry X only, ten Y only and ten neither. An idealised either-target rule covers 90 cells, whereas a both-target rule covers 20. These are recognition-coverage calculations, not measured killing or healthy-tissue selectivity. Expression thresholds, tissue access and cell function still matter.

TNBC describes a breast-cancer subtype, not one universal receptor target. A research programme, a positive stain or a named cell platform does not establish a treatment indication or rank safe recognition strategies. The cited TROP2 work supplies preclinical observations, and the ROR1 phase-I report supplies limited activity and infiltration observations in its actual mixed population. These studies do not supply a comparative clinical-benefit estimate for every antigen-directed product in TNBC. Individual labels and clinical studies define their own disease, regimen and eligibility scope.

Kawalekar’s defined human-CAR experiments linked 4-1BB signalling to outgrowth of CD8 central-memory cells with greater respiratory capacity, fatty-acid oxidation and mitochondrial biogenesis. CD28-containing CARs produced effector-memory cells with a gene-expression pattern consistent with greater glycolysis. These are construct-and-system observations, not a ranking of clinical speed, persistence or safety by domain name. Other receptor parts, preparation, starting-cell state, target and disease setting remain relevant. Ramos simultaneously infused separately tracked second- and third-generation products. Their different expansion and persistence did not let a shared tumour response isolate either product’s clinical contribution.

Relapse mechanisms need separate investigation. Sotillo found CD19 sequence and splicing changes affecting recognition in B-ALL relapse material and experiments. Deng found infusion-product transcriptional features associated with outcomes in a selected cohort of 24 large B-cell lymphoma infusion products; those associations did not prove that one engineered modification would correct every failure.

Conventional surface-antigen recognition can bypass peptide-HLA presentation; specialized peptide-HLA-targeting CARs retain the relevant HLA and antigen-processing requirements.
strengths: Antigen-directed recognition in engineered T cells
Established uses for specific products in selected blood cancers
limitations: Shared healthy-tissue targets and inflammatory, neurologic or blood-count harms
Manufacturing, access and cost depend on the product and setting
Antigen heterogeneity, cell state, tissue access and local inhibition

records.name: CD4 T-cell subsets
records.tldr: CD4 T cells can develop different response programmes. Signals, gene activity and measured function help describe a programme; a single marker does not establish what the cell does.
records.summary:
CD4 T-cell subsets are differentiation programmes shaped by antigen recognition, cytokines and gene regulation. Conventional naive CD4 cells recognize peptide-HLA class II during priming, often on dendritic cells. Th1, Th2, Th17, follicular helper and regulatory programmes have characteristic signals, transcription factors and outputs, but these are not permanent job titles or mutually exclusive functional tests. The original Th1/Th2 distinction came from mouse clones in 1986; human tissue can contain mixed programmes.

CD4 help can improve the magnitude and quality of a CD8 response. Bennett’s experiments showed that CD40 signalling on antigen-presenting cells could replace CD4 help in a defined cross-priming system. Cella found that CD40 ligation increased dendritic-cell IL-12, ICAM-1, CD80 and CD86 and their T-cell-stimulating capacity. These support one licensing mechanism, not a requirement that every response follows an identical route.

Alspach’s mouse-tumour work required tumour-antigen-specific CD4 and CD8 responses even when the cancer cells lacked class-II molecules; tumour expression of class-II-restricted antigens was needed at the successful rejection site. In Ott’s phase-I melanoma vaccine trial, six people received personal neoantigens. CD4 responses targeted 58 of 97 neoantigens (60%) and CD8 responses 15 (16%). Four of six had no recurrence at 25 months, but the small uncontrolled study did not isolate clinical efficacy.

In untreated human breast tumours, Gu-Trantien found CXCL13-producing Tfh cells mainly in tertiary-lymphoid-structure germinal centres and an eight-gene signature associated with survival or preoperative-chemotherapy response. That is a prognostic association. DeNardo’s mouse mammary-cancer experiments showed a different possibility: IL-4-producing CD4 cells shaped macrophages that promoted invasion and lung metastasis. Subset identity therefore needs tissue, timing and measured-function context.

notes: A transcription-factor stain is a clue to a programme, not a function test. In defined human cultures, Tran and colleagues induced high FOXP3 expression without suppressive function. Human colorectal tumours also contained functionally distinct FOXP3-positive populations (Saito 2016). T-bet expression alone does not measure interferon-gamma release, and a bulk Th1-related RNA signature is not a count of one cell type. Neither Th1 nor Th2 identity alone establishes benefit or harm across tissue, timing and tumour contexts.

How subsets are measured. Flow cytometry can stain transcription factors and, after stimulation, cytokines inside cells; single-cell RNA sequencing assigns programmes by gene expression; tissue staining for CXCL13 or FOXP3 adds location. Each method defines subsets by its own markers, so labels may not match across studies.

Worked example (inference). A vaccine study reports strong interferon gamma release from CD4 T cells after stimulation with a vaccine peptide, but no CD8 response. That is not necessarily a failure: Th1-like CD4 cells can license dendritic cells and help CD8 responses, and mouse data show CD4 cells are needed for rejection. The result shows a CD4 response under assay conditions; recognition of the tumour and any benefit need separate evidence.

CD4 does not mean helper-only. Oh and colleagues studied 30,604 T cells from seven bladder-cancer patients and found clonally expanded cytotoxic CD4 states; controlled assays demonstrated MHC-class-II-dependent killing of autologous tumour cells and inhibition by regulatory T cells. This human evidence has a defined cancer, assay and target context. It does not make every CD4 cell cytotoxic or replace the separate helper and regulatory measurements.

Th1 programmes are associated with IL-12 and interferon-gamma signalling and the transcription factor T-bet. Cells can produce interferon gamma and IL-2 and support macrophage and CD8 responses against intracellular microbes, including the development of memory responses. A T-bet stain alone does not demonstrate any one of those outputs.

Th2 differentiation in the systems reviewed by Zhu involved IL-4 and IL-2, with GATA3 and characteristic IL-4, IL-5 and IL-13 production. These programmes are studied in parasite and allergic responses. This functional context does not make Th2 identity uniformly harmful or beneficial in a tumour.

Th17 programmes include ROR-gamma-t and IL-17A, IL-17F and IL-22 outputs. Zhu’s 2010 review described efficient TGF-beta/IL-6-driven differentiation in specified cultures and a later role for IL-23 in development or maintenance. Human STAT3-deficiency observations linked deficient Th17 development with susceptibility to bacterial and fungal infections. Culture steering conditions and barrier-defence associations are not a universal human differentiation recipe or an automatic tumour-effect prediction.

Follicular helper programmes include BCL6 and the CXCR5 receptor that supports follicular location, and help germinal-centre B cells, including through IL-21. Human breast-tumour Tfh cells can produce CXCL13. Zhu’s 2010 discussion of IL-6/IL-21 culture conditions described uncertainty at that time; neither those conditions nor one marker define every Tfh cell or its function.

Regulatory programmes help restrain responses and maintain tolerance. FOXP3 is a central regulator, and TGF-beta/IL-2 support induced differentiation in specified experimental systems. IL-10, TGF-beta and CTLA-4-associated interactions can contribute to regulation in context. These are not exclusive outputs of one programme, and the human FOXP3 studies above explain why marker presence needs a separate suppression assay.

records.name: Cell cycle
records.tldr: Cells preparing to divide pass through regulated stages for growth, DNA copying and chromosome separation. Some cells remain functional while outside that cycle.
records.summary: G1 prepares the cell, S copies DNA, and G2 precedes the mitotic phase. Mitosis separates nuclear chromosomes; cytokinesis separates cytoplasm into daughter cells. G0 describes a noncycling state, which need not mean death or loss of function. Cyclins, CDKs and checkpoints regulate transitions, and their alteration can contribute to cancer without making every checkpoint absent or guaranteeing error-free division. Cell-cycle checkpoints and immune checkpoints describe different biological processes.

records.name: Central dogma and molecular information flow
records.tldr: DNA copying, making RNA and making a protein are different processes. Following the route helps identify what each molecular test actually measured.
records.summary: Replication makes DNA from DNA. Transcription uses a DNA template to make RNA. Translation reads the coding sequence of a message in three-base codons to build a polypeptide; the transcript and reading frame matter. Functional noncoding RNAs do not need to become protein. Reverse transcription copies RNA into DNA in relevant viral and retrotransposon contexts. This information-flow map is not a guarantee that every DNA change produces a measured RNA or protein change.

records.name: cGAS-STING innate sensing
records.tldr: cGAS-STING is the cell's alarm for DNA in the wrong place. Radiation, chemotherapy, and ADCs spill DNA into the cytoplasm; cGAS detects it, STING sounds the alarm, and interferon calls in the immune system.
records.summary: Cytosolic double-stranded DNA (from micronuclei after DNA damage, or from dying tumour cells taken up by dendritic cells) is sensed by cGAS, producing cGAMP, which activates STING on the ER, recruiting TBK1 to phosphorylate IRF3 and NF-κB, driving type I interferon and chemokines (CXCL10) that recruit and prime T cells. Explains the immunogenic effects of radiation (abscopal effect), PARP inhibitors, and TOP1-payload ADCs. Tumours silence STING or express ENPP1 (degrades cGAMP). STING agonists as drugs have disappointed; ENPP1 inhibitors and STING-agonist ADCs are being tested. Sensor and messenger are separate steps: in cell experiments cGAS bound DNA in the cytoplasm and made the second messenger cGAMP, which binds and activates STING (Sun et al., 2013), and the presence of DNA does not by itself measure cGAS activity. STING normally sits in the endoplasmic reticulum; in the cells tested it moved to perinuclear compartments on activation, and palmitoylation at the Golgi was essential for activation (Mukai et al., 2016). That is intracellular trafficking, not release of STING as a circulating messenger. The consequence depends on the cell. Host STING was needed for spontaneous CD8 T-cell priming against tumours in mice (Woo et al., 2014). In chromosomally unstable tumour models, ruptured micronuclei spilled DNA into the cytosol and activated cGAS and STING, and continuing chromosome segregation errors promoted invasion and metastasis in a STING-dependent manner (Bakhoum et al., 2018). A later study reported interferon tachyphylaxis and an endoplasmic reticulum stress response downstream of chronic STING activation in such cells, and an association of chromosomal instability and cGAS activation in micronuclei with immune suppression and metastasis in human triple-negative breast cancer (Li et al., 2023). An interferon RNA signal in a tumour sample cannot identify the producing cell or the sensor behind it, and acute and repeated stimulation can differ, which is not a rule that short stimulation helps and long stimulation harms.

records.name: Immune checkpoint inhibitors
records.tldr: Checkpoint inhibitors block specified immune-regulatory interactions. They can support cancer-directed activity and can also cause immune-related injury; benefit depends on the cancer, regimen and setting.
records.summary: Anti-CTLA-4 (ipilimumab), anti-PD-1 (pembrolizumab, nivolumab, cemiplimab, dostarlimab, toripalimab, tislelizumab), anti-PD-L1 (atezolizumab, durvalumab, avelumab), anti-LAG-3 (relatlimab). Approved across >20 tumour types. The U.S. tumour-agnostic pembrolizumab indication covers adult and paediatric patients with unresectable or metastatic MSI-H or dMMR solid tumours, determined by an FDA-authorised test, that have progressed following prior treatment and who have no satisfactory alternative treatment options. The separate colorectal indication covers unresectable or metastatic MSI-H or dMMR colorectal cancer determined by an FDA-authorised test, without that prior-treatment restriction. For the U.S. tumour-agnostic pembrolizumab indication, TMB-H means at least 13 mutations per megabase, determined by an FDA-authorised test, in adult and paediatric patients with unresectable or metastatic solid tumours that have progressed following prior treatment and who have no satisfactory alternative treatment options. Moving earlier: neoadjuvant/perioperative in melanoma, NSCLC, TNBC (KEYNOTE-522), bladder, and MSI-H colorectal (where dostarlimab produced 100% complete responses in rectal cancer without surgery). Immune-related adverse events are the cost.

notes: Checkpoint antibodies interrupt specified inhibitory contacts. PD-1 is a receptor with two partners, PD-L1 and PD-L2; PD-L1 is a distinct molecule found on cancer and non-cancer cells. The pembrolizumab label describes blockade of PD-1 binding to both ligands. Atezolizumab instead binds PD-L1 and blocks its PD-1 and B7.1 interactions; directly blocking PD-L1 does not directly block the separate PD-1/PD-L2 contact. These target-specific descriptions are more precise than treating all checkpoint drugs as one switch.

The pathways also differ inside and between cells. Hui's 2017 biochemical reconstitution and intact-cell experiments found that PD-1-recruited Shp2 preferentially dephosphorylated CD28 over the T-cell receptor, not that CD28 was the only possible affected signal. CTLA-4 and CD28 share CD80 and CD86. Qureshi's human and mouse cell experiments showed CTLA-4 capture and removal of these ligands from an opposing cell, reducing available costimulation. Contact and capture cartoons show these distinct receptor jobs; their molecule counts and positions are schematic, not a complete mechanism or a clinical comparison of blocking antibodies.

CTLA-4 is often emphasised during priming in lymphoid sites and PD-1 during ongoing responses in tissues. These are overlapping emphases, not exclusive addresses: CD28-related regulation can also matter later. LAG-3, TIM-3 and TIGIT have their own biology rather than being interchangeable versions of PD-1. A regulator identified in an experimental model does not establish benefit from blocking it in another population; each intervention needs its own evidence.

KEYNOTE-522 randomised 1,174 people with previously untreated stage II or III triple-negative breast cancer to pembrolizumab or placebo with chemotherapy before surgery, followed by continuation of the assigned antibody or placebo after surgery. At a median follow-up of 75.1 months, estimated 60-month overall survival was 86.6 per cent versus 81.7 per cent. Enrolment did not require PD-L1 positivity. The trial compared the whole perioperative regimen and was not designed to isolate the contribution of each treatment phase. These group results do not predict one person's outcome.

KEYNOTE-355 studied 847 people with previously untreated locally recurrent inoperable or metastatic triple-negative breast cancer. In the PD-L1 combined-positive-score-at-least-10 subgroup, pembrolizumab plus chemotherapy gave median overall survival of 23.0 months versus 16.1 with placebo plus chemotherapy, with a death hazard ratio of 0.73. A median divides a study group in half; it is not an individual forecast. The October 2026 U.S. pembrolizumab label has no PD-L1 qualifier for its high-risk early-stage TNBC regimen, while its advanced TNBC indications with chemotherapy or sacituzumab govitecan specify CPS at least 10 and an FDA-authorised test. The sacituzumab combination is a separate labelled regimen, not the KEYNOTE-355 comparison. Population, regimen, scoring context and evidence must stay together.

Checkpoint blockade changes an inhibitory interaction; it does not install a new recognition receptor or reconstruct required HLA machinery that has been genetically lost. That last statement concerns missing machinery, not a claim that checkpoint treatment can never affect regulated HLA expression. Recognition, access and cell state remain separate dependencies. Vaccines, engineered cell receptors and cytokines change different inputs, and a plausible combination still needs regimen-specific benefit and safety evidence.

In a fictional sample containing PD-1-positive T cells, staining does not identify every cell's target, functional state or capacity to respond to an antibody. It does not show that all those cells are exhausted or that a drug will awaken all of them. Similarly, interrupting inhibition cannot alone solve a missing target-display component. Checkpoint biology, drug action, marker measurement and prediction of clinical benefit are separate claims.

The multiple-controls analogy has two possible branches: interrupting regulation can support useful cancer-directed activity and can also injure healthy tissue. Neither outcome is guaranteed for a person. Normal checkpoint regulation helps limit immune injury, and immune-related adverse events can involve several organs. Assess activity, durability and harms in the relevant population rather than equating more immune activity with exclusively tumour-directed benefit.

Colorectal cancer: the sharpest biomarker split in oncology. In mismatch repair deficient disease, responses run from 31% (single-agent nivolumab, previously treated) to 68% pathological complete response (four weeks of neoadjuvant nivolumab plus ipilimumab); in microsatellite-stable disease, the phase 3 test of atezolizumab with or without a MEK inhibitor was no better than regorafenib (Eng 2019). The only credible microsatellite-stable signal is the Fc-enhanced CTLA-4 antibody botensilimab with balstilimab, 17% response in 101 evaluable patients (Bullock 2024).

Lung cancer: NICE NG122 places checkpoint treatment at four separate points, which is why the same side-effect list keeps reappearing. Before and after surgery: nivolumab with chemotherapy (1.6.8), durvalumab with platinum chemotherapy (1.6.9) and pembrolizumab with platinum chemotherapy (1.6.10) for resectable disease. After chemoradiotherapy: durvalumab for locally advanced unresectable disease with PD-L1 on 1 percent or more of tumour cells (1.6.18), and for limited-stage small-cell disease that has not progressed (1.10.6). For advanced disease: the treatment pathways organised by PD-L1 below or at or above 50 percent. For extensive-stage small-cell disease: durvalumab or atezolizumab added to chemotherapy (1.11.3).

Lung cancer: the biomarker story in one line is that PD-L1 selects and nothing else does reliably. A 50% threshold by 22C3 supported first-line monotherapy where a 5% threshold by 28-8 did not (Reck 2016, Carbone 2017), tumour mutational burden failed once chemotherapy was added (Garassino 2023), and STK11 and KEAP1 predict poor benefit only in KRAS-mutant tumours (Ricciuti 2022). In small-cell disease the inflamed transcriptional subtype gains most from adding immunotherapy to chemotherapy, which is the first credible explanation of why the benefit is confined to a minority (Gay 2021).

Lymphoma: the contrast between Hodgkin lymphoma and everything else is genetic rather than mysterious. The 9p24.1 amplicon carries both PD-1 ligand genes and JAK2, which induces them further, so one copy-number event raises the brake twice over; 97% of 108 classical Hodgkin lymphomas carried concordant alterations of the two loci (Green 2010, Roemer 2016). PD-1 blockade gave an objective response in 20 of 23 heavily pre-treated Hodgkin patients (Ansell 2015). In B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma outside the mediastinal group, single-agent checkpoint blockade does very little. Within the responsive group, what predicts complete remission is expression of MHC class II rather than class I on the Hodgkin and Reed-Sternberg cells, which points to a CD4 T cell as the effector (Roemer 2018).

records.name: Hot vs cold tumours
records.tldr: Hot, excluded and desert describe where specified immune cells were found in sampled tissue. Their location alone does not establish tumour recognition, effective killing or benefit from a particular drug.
records.summary:
An inflamed or hot pattern has specified immune cells within sampled tumour regions. In an excluded pattern, cells concentrate in surrounding stroma or at a boundary with less entry into malignant nests. A desert has few relevant cells in the examined regions. Cold is used for desert alone or for both desert and excluded patterns, so state the definition. A macrophage-rich sample is not automatically T-cell inflamed.

These are observations about identity and location. Some infiltrating T cells recognize viral or other non-cancer antigens; others restrain responses. Region, specimen, disease site and sampling time matter, and treatment can change the pattern. Neither a small biopsy nor a pattern label describes every site in a person or selects an immunotherapy. Exclusion suggests questions about recruitment, vessels, matrix and local cells, rather than proving one causal wall.

Equal counts can conceal different locations. Region outlines do not prove a physical barrier, these counts do not describe all mononuclear cells used in stromal TIL scoring, and they cannot be converted to an sTIL area percentage. The example depicts neither lymph-node follicles nor tertiary lymphoid organization and supplies no clinical cutoff or response rate.

Routine pathology can score a defined infiltrate, multiplex imaging adds selected cell identities and coordinates, and mixed-tissue gene expression describes programmes without directly retaining each cell’s location. Report the preparation, section, sampled regions, staining and cell-assignment rules, regional variation, output and denominator. Descriptive labels, cells per area and method-defined stromal scores are different outputs. Sectioning and staining use finite tissue. Damage, staining error, incorrect boundaries and an unrepresentative region can limit the result. A research classifier needs separate validation for a clinical selection use.

In Loi’s pooled analysis of 2,148 early TNBC patients given anthracycline-based adjuvant chemotherapy with or without taxanes, each 10 percentage-point increase in stromal TILs was associated with iDFS HR 0.87 and OS HR 0.84. This is prognosis in that population, not proof of additional checkpoint-drug benefit by hot/cold category. Taube’s tissue study also supports coexistence of lymphocyte infiltration and induced inhibitory PD-L1; hot does not mean every later immune step succeeds.

Pancreatic examples have specific settings. Feig’s pancreatic mouse model connected FAP-positive fibroblast CXCL12 with T-cell exclusion; Yamamoto’s work identified autophagy-dependent class-I degradation and tested immune rescue in mice. These are not measurements of every human pancreatic tumour. Royal’s 27-person ipilimumab study reported no RECIST responses but one delayed regression after initial progression. O’Reilly’s 65-person metastatic study reported objective response rates of 3.1% with durvalumab plus tremelimumab and 0% with durvalumab alone, without meeting its expansion threshold. These historical studies do not establish a complete treatment-selection rule or prove that one molecular subgroup is the only possible responder population.

records.name: Costimulation
records.tldr: Additional receptor contacts help shape a T cell's response to a recognised target.
records.summary:
Costimulation supplies supporting interactions alongside antigen recognition. CD28 engagement by B7 supported proliferation and interleukin-2 responses in Linsley and colleagues' controlled experiments. CTLA-4 shares CD80/CD86 ligands with CD28 and can remove these ligands from opposing cells by trans-endocytosis, reducing available costimulation. Supporting contacts do not determine a new antigen specificity.

Compare the same recognition stimulus with and without supporting contacts, with viable-cell, stimulus and pathway controls. Measure division, cytokines and killing separately. Identical peptide-HLA displays can have different supporting contexts. CD28 dependence of PD-1 rescue was demonstrated in chronic-infection and tumour-bearing mouse systems; proliferating blood CD8 cells after treatment in lung-cancer patients were predominantly CD28-positive. This does not validate CD28 abundance as a universal treatment-selection test. Engineered supporting domains require product-specific safety and efficacy evidence.

notes: Costimulation consists of additional supporting receptor interactions alongside antigen recognition, affecting activation, survival, division or differentiation. CD28 is one example, not the whole category or a universal threshold. The same peptide-HLA stimulus can receive different support without changing antigen specificity. Blocking inhibition and adding support are distinct interventions.

Compare the same recognition stimulus with and without a specified supporting interaction, using recognition-only, viable-cell and inhibitory-context controls. Measure division, cytokines and killing separately; marker abundance does not establish causal signalling. Engineered intracellular supporting domains change receptor architecture but require product-specific persistence, safety and efficacy tests.

records.name: Circulating tumour DNA (ctDNA)
records.tldr: Circulating tumour DNA (ctDNA) consists of fragments of DNA shed by tumour cells into the blood, detectable with sensitive sequencing.
records.summary: Circulating tumour DNA (ctDNA) is made up of DNA fragments shed by tumour cells into the bloodstream, where they form only a small fraction of all cell-free DNA and are detected with sensitive sequencing. Its uses span genotyping for companion diagnostics, tracking resistance mutations such as EGFR T790M and ESR1, molecular residual disease, early detection and response monitoring. Shedding varies with tumour type and burden, and clonal haematopoiesis can confound results. The term underpins the Liquid biopsy (ctDNA), MRD / molecular residual disease testing and Multi-cancer early detection (MCED) technologies, and it appears in the SERENA-6, CIRCULATE-Japan and IMvigor011 trials and in ideas on molecular-progression switching beyond ESR1 and HPV ctDNA to guide cervical cancer therapy.

notes: Detection depends on stage and tumour type: with digital PCR-based methods in 640 patients, ctDNA was found in more than 75% of people with advanced pancreatic, ovarian, colorectal, bladder, gastro-oesophageal, breast, melanoma, hepatocellular and head and neck cancers, and in fewer than 50% of primary brain, renal, prostate or thyroid cancers. In localised disease it was found in 73% of colorectal, 57% of gastro-oesophageal, 48% of pancreatic and 50% of breast adenocarcinomas, and it was often present in people with no detectable circulating tumour cells (Bettegowda 2014). The assay, specimen and population are part of each figure.

ctDNA is a subset of cell-free DNA, and not every plasma variant is tumour-derived: in paired plasma and white-blood-cell sequencing, 53.2% of cfDNA mutations in 124 people with metastatic cancer and 81.6% in 47 people without cancer had features of clonal haematopoiesis (Razavi 2019). A ctDNA result is also a quantity with a unit (molecules per millilitre, a fraction, or a call), and the same number means different things under each.

Lung cancer: plasma genotyping at diagnosis is non-inferior to tissue for finding a guideline biomarker (27.3% against 21.3% in 282 patients), has 100% positive predictive value for the alterations with approved drugs, returns in 9 days against 15, and raises detection by 48% when added to tissue (Leighl 2019). Clinical sensitivity against tissue is 80%, so a negative plasma result rules nothing out and the guideline permits plasma to rule in only (Lindeman 2018). Serial plasma after starting treatment also separates the patients whose resistant clone was already present, within three weeks (Oxnard 2018).

records.name: ctDNA units, fractions and concentrations
records.tldr: A ctDNA result is a number with a unit. Molecules per millilitre, parts per million and allele fraction answer different questions, so a printed number means nothing until its unit and denominator are known.
records.summary:
Circulating tumour DNA (ctDNA) can be reported as a concentration, as a fraction, or as a yes or no call, and the three are not interchangeable. A concentration counts tumour-attributed molecules in a stated volume of plasma. One example is mean tumour molecules per millilitre (MTM/mL), which the I-SPY 2 breast-cancer study of Magbanua and colleagues used for ctDNA across tracked variants. A fraction divides tumour-attributed molecules by a stated total, such as all evaluated alleles at one position (variant allele fraction, VAF) or all evaluated DNA (an estimated tumour fraction). Parts per million (PPM) is a fraction multiplied by one million, so the number is only as meaningful as the fraction it scales: 0.01% is 100 PPM, and 0.00024% is 2.4 PPM, the lowest allele fraction Santonja and colleagues reported for ctDNA detection in breast cancer.

Concentration and fraction can move apart. If two equal one-millilitre aliquots each hold the same number of tumour molecules but one holds more background cell-free DNA, the concentration is unchanged and the fraction falls. A detection call and a reliable amount are also different claims, because the detection limit and the quantitation range are validated separately. Nothing here gives a conversion between assays: MTM/mL cannot be turned into PPM from the printed result, and a VAF of 100 PPM at one variant is not a tumour fraction of 100 PPM.

notes: Method card, what it measures: the quantity an assay states, either a count of tumour-attributed molecules per volume of plasma (a concentration), a share of a named total (a fraction), or a call. How: sequencing or PCR on one finite plasma aliquot, then a calculation the laboratory defines. Keep the unit, the denominator and the assay version attached to every value.

Table, MTM/mL: mean tumour molecules per millilitre of plasma under the assay's own calculation across its tracked features. Boundary: a concentration estimated from tracked features, not the number of cancer cells per millilitre and not a share of anything.

Table, PPM: parts per million, a fraction multiplied by one million, so 1 PPM is 0.0001% and 100 PPM is 0.01%. Boundary: name the fraction being scaled, because 100 PPM of variant alleles, of evaluated DNA and of tumour-attributed molecules are three different claims.

Table, variant allele fraction: the share of evaluated alleles at one position that carry a stated variant. Boundary: it depends on copy number, on which clones carry the variant and on the measurement, and a variant present in a blood-cell clone counts the same way as one from a tumour.

Table, tumour fraction: an estimated share of evaluated DNA attributable to tumour. Boundary: it is a model output that rests on the method and its calibration, and it is not automatically any single variant's VAF.

Fictional arithmetic, concentration against fraction: two equal 1 mL aliquots each hold 4 tumour-attributed molecules. Aliquot A also holds 16 background molecules, so 4 of 20 is 20% and the concentration is 4 molecules per mL. Aliquot B holds 36 background molecules, so 4 of 40 is 10% and the concentration is still 4 per mL. More background lowered the fraction and left the concentration alone. These toy shares are not a VAF, an estimated tumour fraction or MTM/mL.

Fictional arithmetic, rescaling: a VAF of 0.01% at Variant R equals 100 PPM of variant-supporting alleles. That does not make a tumour fraction of 100 PPM, and a second report of 0.2 MTM/mL is a concentration, so 100 and 0.2 cannot be compared or converted without the methods and calibration of both assays.

Method limit, detection against quantitation: a qualifying detection call and a reliable numerical amount have separate validation criteria. A detected value below the validated quantitative range does not support an exact fold change, and extra decimal places do not create precision.

Method limit, finite input: the plasma volume drawn is not the volume or the number of molecules recovered and evaluated. Low molecular counts, changes in background DNA, poor recovery or incompatible calibration all limit comparison across assays, and a printed zero is not a count of zero cancer cells anywhere in the body.

Evidence read: in Magbanua's 84-patient pilot of neoadjuvant treatment, ctDNA in MTM/mL was correlated with MRI functional tumour volume at every time point (Spearman rho 0.42 to 0.49). Santonja's comparison reported allele fractions down to 2.4 PPM for hybrid-capture sequencing of 1,347 to 7,491 tumour-identified mutations and 4.7 PPM for multiplex PCR of 21 to 47 structural variants. Each figure belongs to its assay and cohort.

A trend also needs the collection time, treatment context, assay version and quantitative range. In its November 2024 drug-development guidance, FDA asks for precision, accuracy and detection-limit evaluation across relevant inputs and cut-offs, using representative clinical specimens and appropriately comparable reference material. A printed number below another assay's nominal detection limit does not establish that the other assay would miss that sample: the measured quantity, specimen, input, recovery and calling rules may differ. A reference-material result is not automatically a clinical sensitivity estimate.

Consider a fictional assay estimating tumour fraction at 6 parts per million (PPM) and then 2 PPM. Both samples are called detected, but the second is below the assay's reliable quantitation range. The printed estimates fall by two-thirds; they do not establish that the cancer volume fell by two-thirds. Retain the qualifying calls and uncertainty, because shedding and background DNA can change the signal. A second method reporting molecules per millilitre cannot simply be placed on this fraction scale. Even a matching unit label does not establish matching calibration. Keeping serial methods and input comparable helps interpretation without removing biological variation.

The blank, detection and quantitation limits answer different questions. The blank limit is the highest apparent analyte concentration expected from replicate samples with no analyte; the detection limit is the lowest concentration reliably distinguished from that background; the quantitation limit is the lowest concentration meeting predefined bias and imprecision goals (Armbruster and Pry, 2008). Quantitation and detection limits may coincide or differ. A qualifying detection below a validated quantitative range supports presence more strongly than an exact fold change. For a read-based variant allele fraction, the denominator is informative reads covering that locus, not cancer cells or plasma volume; keep a molecule-based method's own definition instead.

records.name: Cytokine
records.tldr: Small proteins immune cells use to talk to each other: alarms, recruitment calls, growth orders and stand-down signals. Some are cancer drugs, and a flood of them is the danger of certain immunotherapies.
records.summary: Interleukins, interferons, tumour necrosis factor and chemokines each act on cells carrying the matching receptor; IL-2 drives T-cell growth and was one of the first immunotherapies (aldesleukin), interferon-alpha was used in melanoma and leukaemia, and engineered cytokines aim to keep the benefit while losing the toxicity. Tumours secrete cytokines that recruit suppressive cells and drive inflammation, and IL-6 is a major driver of cancer cachexia. When CAR-T cells or T-cell engagers activate en masse they release cytokines in a surge (cytokine release syndrome), treated by blocking IL-6 with tocilizumab. A cytokine name does not specify one outcome: one cytokine can act differently on different receiving cells (pleiotropy), different signals can give overlapping outputs (redundancy), and receptor availability, concentration, exposure time and cell state all shape the response. A review of receptor biology said that all cytokines, to a greater or lesser extent, show pleiotropy (multiple biological actions) and redundancy (shared biological actions), and proposed that redundancy might be explained by related cytokines using a common receptor subunit, while pleiotropy requires that receptors exert different activities on different cells (Nicola, 1994). Different IL-2 and anti-IL-2 antibody complexes selectively expanded CD8 T cells or CD4 regulatory T cells in mice, so the formulation and the receiving cells mattered (Boyman et al., 2006). Chemokines help direct cell movement through gradients: in mouse skin an immobilised CCL21 gradient guided dendritic cells towards lymphatic vessels, and displacing or swamping it abolished directed migration (Weber et al., 2013), but movement also needs a compatible receptor and a traversable route. Measurements answer different questions: a concentration in picograms per millilitre of a named fluid, the percentage of a defined cell gate making a protein after stimulation, and RNA expression are different layers, a blood concentration does not reconstruct a tumour gradient, and two preparations can share an average (0 and 20, or 10 and 10, picograms per millilitre both average 10) while differing in spatial pattern. Intracellular cytokine staining usually involves a stimulation of a few hours (4 to 6 hours was usually sufficient to detect interferon gamma and tumour necrosis factor), a block on secretion with brefeldin A or monensin so that the protein stays inside the cell, and negative and positive controls (Cossarizza et al., 2019). Calibration and a detection limit belong in the same report; that is OnCo's reporting advice and not a finding of the cited guideline. Chemokines are a family of cytokines and not a separate category, a growth-support signal such as IL-2 does not choose the antigen a T cell recognises, and more signal is not automatically more useful or safer immunity. For interferons, timing and the receiving cell mattered in mouse experiments: endogenous type I interferon was needed to prevent the growth of carcinogen-induced and transplanted tumours and acted through host blood-lineage cells (Dunn et al., 2005), whereas prolonged interferon signalling in experimental tumours maintained a resistance programme to checkpoint blockade (Benci et al., 2016). That a signal is tumour-associated does not by itself make it a safe target; this is OnCo's boundary statement and not a cited finding.
