records.name: Dendritic-cell cross-presentation (cDC1)
records.tldr: Cross-presentation displays externally acquired protein fragments on class I HLA. Initial activation of a naive T cell is a further step called cross-priming.
records.summary:
Class I HLA commonly displays fragments of proteins made within the presenting cell. Cross-presentation means displaying externally acquired antigen on class I HLA. Naive CD8 T-cell priming is a further activation step requiring an appropriate presenting cell and supporting signals; tumour-cell display alone does not establish priming. The subset specialised for this is the type 1 conventional dendritic cell (cDC1): CD8alpha+ and CD103+ in mice, CD141 (BDCA-3)+ in humans, dependent on FLT3 ligand and the transcription factor BATF3 for development, internalising necrotic-cell material through CLEC9A (DNGR-1), a receptor for polymerised actin, and expressing the chemokine receptor XCR1, which favours contact with CD8 T cells (Alfaro et al., 2013).

The in vivo proof came from Batf3-deficient mice (Hildner et al., Science 2008): they lacked CD8alpha+ dendritic cells, their dendritic cells were defective in cross-presentation, and they failed to reject highly immunogenic syngeneic tumours. In mouse melanoma, CD103+ dendritic cells were the only antigen-presenting cells carrying intact antigen to lymph nodes and priming tumour-specific CD8 T cells, and they were required for PD-L1 blockade to work; expanding them with FLT3 ligand and activating them with intratumoral poly I:C improved responses to PD-L1 and BRAF inhibition (Salmon et al., Immunity 2016). This is why a scarcity of cDC1 in a tumour is read as one cause of a cold, checkpoint-resistant tumour, and why vaccine designs target antigen to cDC1 receptors such as CLEC9A, or expand and activate these cells, rather than relying on bulk monocyte-derived dendritic cells.

Cross-presentation names a display process, whereas cross-priming names the activation of naive CD8 T cells through it, which needs supporting signals and its own readout. Direct presentation remains possible: a dendritic cell that receives vaccine messenger RNA and makes the protein itself presents it directly. A cell can also acquire already assembled peptide-HLA complexes from another cell (cross-dressing), which does not show processing by the recipient (Wakim and Bevan, Nature 2011, PMID 21455179, mouse viral infection). External antigen on class II is not cross-presentation.

records.name: Dendritic cells
records.tldr: Dendritic cells are immune cells that collect pieces of material from their surroundings and show them to T cells, and the signals they give at that moment help decide whether a T cell is switched on or held back. Counting them in a tumour sample does not show that they have taught T cells to recognise the cancer.
records.summary: Dendritic cells acquire material from their surroundings or make antigen themselves, process proteins and display fragments on HLA molecules, where a matching T-cell receptor can recognise a peptide and HLA pair. Cross-presentation is the route that places acquired material on class I, and class II presentation, usually of acquired proteins to CD4 T cells, is a separate route. They are a family of subsets with overlapping jobs. Conventional type 1 cells (cDC1) are particularly important for cross-presentation: mice lacking the transcription factor Batf3 lost CD8-alpha-positive dendritic cells, their dendritic cells were defective in cross-presentation, and they rejected highly immunogenic tumours less well (Hildner et al., 2008). Human CD141-positive dendritic cells, activated with poly I:C, cross-presented soluble antigen and antigen from necrotic virus-infected cells better than CD1c-positive cells (Jongbloed et al., 2010). Conventional type 2 cells are usually studied for class II presentation to CD4 T cells, and plasmacytoid cells for type I interferon responses. In a review, plasmacytoid cells are described as producing large amounts of interferon alpha, while the contribution of CD11b-positive conventional cells to CD4 T-cell priming in vivo was still described as to be determined (Merad et al., 2013). The same review describes conventional cells as inducing immunity to foreign antigens and enforcing tolerance to self-antigens, and migration-linked maturation as raising MHC class II and costimulatory molecules, with cytokine production added when migration follows inflammation. In mice, antigen delivered to dendritic cells in the steady state led to brief T-cell activation followed by loss and unresponsiveness of the T cells, and adding an anti-CD40 antibody changed the outcome to prolonged activation (Hawiger et al., 2001). For conventional type 2 cells, a review of dendritic cells in T-cell programming reported that they were most often found to be required for CD4 T-cell priming in mice, with T helper 1 differentiation as an exception in which type 1 cells were often required, and noted that type 2 cells can be difficult to distinguish from monocyte-derived cells because markers overlap (Eisenbarth, 2019); another review said that specific depletion of type 2 cells was still needed to confirm their unique role in priming CD4 T cells (Durai and Murphy, 2016). Single-cell sequencing of human blood found six dendritic-cell and four monocyte subtypes, including a population that resembles plasmacytoid cells but potently activates T cells, so one positive marker is weaker evidence than a supported subset assignment (Villani et al., 2017).

Immature and mature describe response-related states, and maturation can change antigen handling, costimulation, cytokines and movement without turning one subset into another. Presentation can support tolerance as well as activation, so antigen uptake, mature-looking markers and functional priming are separate observations. Where cells meet also matters. Some dendritic cells carry antigen from tissue to a draining lymph node, while resident cells in the node take up soluble antigen that arrives in lymph through conduits before migrating cells arrive (Sixt et al., 2005, mouse). In mouse tumours, cDC1 accumulation often depended on natural killer cells that produced the chemokines CCL5 and XCL1, tumour prostaglandin E2 disrupted that axis, and in human cancers the same transcripts tracked natural killer and cDC1 signatures and were associated with longer overall survival, an association (Böttcher et al., 2018).

Three limits matter for tumours. A vaccine that reaches a dendritic cell may make the encoded protein inside it, and that class I display need not be cross-presentation. A dendritic cell can supply a priming opportunity, but the cancer cell must itself display a recognisable target for an antigen-specific CD8 T cell to attack it, so successful presentation does not repair a cancer cell's loss of an HLA allele. And a low count in one biopsy does not show that no priming happened in another compartment. Subsets are identified by flow cytometry, tissue staining, spatial and RNA methods, but whether a cell presents a defined target and stimulates a suitable responder needs a functional test with controls.

records.name: Endogenous T-cell therapy
records.tldr: A treatment that finds the rare T cells in a patient's own blood that already recognise the cancer, grows large numbers of them in the laboratory without changing their genes, and infuses them back.
records.summary: Yee, Lizee and Schueneman describe three ways of adoptive T-cell transfer: tumour-infiltrating lymphocytes taken from a biopsy; lymphocytes redirected by a chimeric antigen receptor or T-cell receptor; and the isolation and expansion of often low-frequency endogenous T cells reactive to tumour antigens from the peripheral blood, which they call endogenous T-cell (ETC) therapy (Cancer Journal 2015). It needs specialised methods to isolate and expand very low-frequency tumour-reactive T cells from blood, and the authors note that a trial can be started quickly once a tumour-associated target epitope has been identified (Cancer Journal 2015). The early melanoma trials at Fred Hutchinson Cancer Research Center infused such cells as clones against MART-1, gp100, tyrosinase and NY-ESO-1.

records.name: HLA (human leukocyte antigen) and MHC
records.tldr: HLA molecules sit on cells and hold up small pieces of the cell's proteins for T cells to inspect. A T cell reads the fragment together with the particular HLA version holding it.
records.summary:
Human leukocyte antigen (HLA) is the human major histocompatibility complex (MHC) system, with two main classes of peptide-display molecule. Classical class I (HLA-A, HLA-B, HLA-C) has a heavy chain, beta-2 microglobulin (B2M) and a bound peptide, is found on most nucleated cells, usually displays peptides from proteins made inside the cell and is read by CD8 T cells. Class II (HLA-DR, HLA-DP, HLA-DQ) has alpha and beta chains with a bound peptide, is mainly on professional antigen-presenting cells (expression can be induced elsewhere), usually displays proteins processed in vesicles, often acquired from outside, and is read by CD4 T cells. These are common routes, not exclusive lists: cross-presentation puts externally acquired antigen on class I without making it class II, and a CD4 response is not proof of matching class I tumour display. CD4 and CD8 are coreceptors and usual recognition partners, not guarantees of cell function. Structural work shows the T-cell receptor lying across the peptide and HLA together (Garboczi et al., 1996), CD8 contacting the class I alpha2 and alpha3 domains and B2M (Gao et al., 1997) and CD4 engaging a separate class II region (Yin et al., 2012); these constructs do not define universal angles or functions.

HLA alleles are shared across people, and a person inherits a combination that is not necessarily unique. Each person inherits two copies each of HLA-A, HLA-B and HLA-C, so a cell can display up to six classical class I variants at once. The IPD-IMGT/HLA statistics page read on 9 November 2026 listed 46,146 HLA alleles, 31,311 class I and 14,835 class II (9,457 HLA-A, 11,328 HLA-B and 9,580 HLA-C alleles). Binding predictors estimate whether a peptide can fit a specified allele's groove, but processing, transport, loading and surface expression decide whether it is displayed. Sarkizova et al. (2020) profiled more than 185,000 peptides eluted from 95 mono-allelic cell lines to learn allele-specific motifs and build prediction models; that is allele-level data, not proof of any cell's display. Kaur et al. (2017) showed that HLA-C surface expression varies across individuals in an allele-specific manner, influenced by the structure of the peptide-binding cleft and peptide diversity; Apps and colleagues found lower HLA-C than HLA-A/B in the analysed healthy-donor peripheral blood lymphocytes with the A*02:01/B*44:02/C*05:01 haplotype; the magnitude differed between flow cytometry and mass spectrometry. This is a defined comparison, not a universal hierarchy. The small HLA-C peptide share observed by Schellens and colleagues in four B lymphoblastoid cell lines was also affected by their assignment method, which gave HLA-A/B precedence; it is not a universal biological fraction.

In cancer, class I HLA shows peptides to CD8 T cells and is also the main ligand for inhibitory receptors on natural killer cells, so losing it can hide a tumour from T cells while removing a brake on NK cells. HLA-E and HLA-G are nonclassical and vary little between people; HLA-E presents leader peptides from other class I molecules and binds the NK receptor CD94/NKG2A (Braud et al., 1998, with HLA-E tetramers). Tumours can lose a presenting allele (HLA loss of heterozygosity), alter processing or reduce expression, and allele-specific loss differs from complete loss of conventional class I display; targets on retained alleles may remain possible. Tran et al. (2016) documented a colorectal cancer lesion that progressed after T-cell therapy against mutant KRAS G12D, which had lost the chromosome 6 haplotype encoding the restricting HLA-C*08:02; this shows escape in one patient, not a rate. Typing, protein expression, recovered peptide, recognition and killing are different observations, and a conventional surface-target engager avoids peptide-HLA dependence while a peptide-HLA-directed engager keeps it.

B2M is the light chain of classical class I and does not span the membrane; class II contains no B2M, so CD4 T-cell recognition can remain when B2M is lost. B2M also partners other class I-like molecules: UniProt records heterotrimers with HLA-E, HLA-G, HLA-F and MR1 and lists CD1 interactions, and a B2M mutation caused deficiency of the neonatal Fc receptor FcRn in two siblings (Wani et al., 2006), so complete B2M loss can remove more than classical class I. Loss of one HLA allele can leave other presenting alleles usable, whereas loss of functional B2M impairs many class I targets at once, so several peptides on different alleles are not independent protection. A B2M variant, low RNA, absent surface class I and a blood B2M concentration are different observations: one variant does not show complete functional loss, and blood B2M does not count tumour peptide-HLA complexes. Zaretsky et al. (2016) linked a truncating B2M mutation to lost surface class I in one melanoma relapse after PD-1 blockade, which is a mechanism in that setting, not a frequency. Reduced class I display does not guarantee NK-cell killing, because activating signals are still needed.

records.name: Immunohistochemistry (IHC)
records.tldr: Staining a tissue slice with antibodies so a protein shows up in colour under the microscope.
records.summary: Immunohistochemistry (IHC) uses antibody binding and signal development to show a selected protein in a prepared tissue section. Interpretation retains which cells and compartments stain, the intensity and distribution, and the named marker-specific method. A percentage, intensity category or composite score can describe different aspects of the result. Fixation, retrieval, controls, sampling and observer variation affect interpretation. Automated quantification also needs validation for its marker, specimens and intended use. A research stain or generic score does not replace a validated clinical selection assay.

notes: There is no universal IHC scoring scale or positivity threshold. Retain antibody clone, retrieval and detection method, controls, eligible cells, subcellular location, intensity, distribution and intended use. A research stain does not automatically replace a clinical selection assay.

An H-score under the intensity-weighted convention is weak-cell percentage plus twice moderate-cell percentage plus three times strong-cell percentage, on a 0 to 300 scale. Fictional example: 50 unstained, 10 weak, 20 moderate and 20 strong cells out of 100 give 50% positive and H-score 110. Neither is a molecule count.

Bulk receptor abundance and staining mainly on blood vessels can both be correct: one measures a mixture and the other locates signal. Neither establishes target accessibility or treatment benefit. Staining also does not establish protein activity or cancer-cell dependence on that protein.

IHC makes selected proteins visible through antibody binding and signal development in a prepared section. Specificity, retrieval, detection, positive controls, internal controls and background matter. Nuclear and membrane signals answer different questions. Multiplex fluorescence adds markers but still needs validated antibody performance and cell-boundary assignment.

In the conventional Allred scheme, proportion categories are 0 for no positive cells, 1 for less than 1%, 2 for 1% to 10%, 3 for 11% to 33%, 4 for 34% to 66% and 5 for 67% to 100%. Intensity is 0 for absent staining or 1, 2 and 3 for weak, moderate and strong staining. The total is 0 or 2 to 8. In a fictional separate example, 30% positive cells with moderate staining give 3 + 2 = 5. These integer bins are a named convention, not a universal positivity rule.

Equal H-scores can conceal different intensity distributions. A negative clinical category does not establish zero protein molecules. HER2 and hormone-receptor assays have marker-specific reporting rules; current CAP breast reporting retains percentage and intensity even when an optional composite score is given.

A useful IHC result identifies the block, fixation and section, antibody clone, retrieval and detection system, eligible cells and scored compartment. Cutting and staining use finite tissue. Report the percentage, intensity, location and named scoring scale, together with expected-positive tissue, relevant internal controls and background assessment. Poor preservation, nonspecific binding, few eligible cells, heterogeneous staining and observer variation can limit interpretation. Validation must fit the assay and its intended use; a research measurement is not automatically a clinical selection test.

records.name: Immune checkpoint
records.tldr: Brakes on the immune system that stop T cells attacking healthy tissue. Tumours pull these brakes to protect themselves; checkpoint inhibitor drugs release them so T cells can attack the cancer.
records.summary: PD-1 on a T cell, when it meets PD-L1 on another cell, tells the T cell to stand down; CTLA-4 is often emphasised earlier, during priming, and PD-1 during ongoing responses in tissues, but these are overlapping emphases and not separate addresses. Reviews describe CTLA-4 as acting early in lymph nodes and PD-1 later in peripheral tissues, while CTLA-4 is also expressed on activated effector CD8 T cells (Buchbinder and Desai, 2016; Pardoll, 2012), and LAG-3, TIM-3 and TIGIT as co-inhibitory receptors with their own specialised functions (Anderson et al., 2016), so the early or late shorthand for CTLA-4 and PD-1 should not be stretched to them. Tumours coat themselves in PD-L1 and exploit this, and antibodies that block PD-1 (pembrolizumab, nivolumab), PD-L1 (atezolizumab, durvalumab) or CTLA-4 (ipilimumab) restore the attack, producing durable remissions in melanoma, lung, kidney, bladder and many other cancers since 2011. The price is autoimmune side effects when the brakes come off everywhere, and only a minority of patients respond, which drives the search for newer checkpoints (LAG-3, TIGIT) and combinations. The 'checkpoint' in 'cell-cycle checkpoint' is an unrelated concept. The checkpoints work through different contacts and are not interchangeable versions of PD-1. In reconstitution and cell experiments, PD-1 engaged by PD-L1 recruited the phosphatase Shp2, which dephosphorylated the co-receptor CD28 in preference to the T-cell receptor (Hui et al., 2017). PD-1 has two ligands, PD-L1 and PD-L2, and PD-L1 is found on leukocytes and on non-haematopoietic cells in non-lymphoid tissues as well as on cancer cells, and can be induced by interferon gamma (Buchbinder and Desai, 2016). In the current US prescribing information for pembrolizumab, the indication for high-risk early-stage triple-negative breast cancer (chemotherapy before surgery, then pembrolizumab alone afterwards) carries no PD-L1 qualifier, whereas the indications for locally recurrent unresectable or metastatic disease (with chemotherapy) and for unresectable locally advanced or metastatic disease (with sacituzumab govitecan) name a PD-L1 combined positive score of 10 or more as determined by an FDA-authorized test. That describes how the approved uses are worded and is not a trial finding about who benefits. CTLA-4 shares the ligands CD80 and CD86 with CD28 and can capture them from opposing cells by trans-endocytosis, so the neighbouring cell has fewer costimulatory ligands to offer (Qureshi et al., 2011). These descriptions concern the receptors' own contacts and are not a model of what a blocking antibody does or a prediction of clinical benefit. LAG-3 selectively recognised stable complexes of peptide and MHC class II and suppressed T cells responding to them, without recognising every class II complex or blocking CD4 binding (Maruhashi et al., 2018). Bat3 bound to and repressed TIM-3 function and protected helper T cells from galectin-9-mediated death, and in cell-line co-expression experiments galectin-9 abolished Bat3 binding to TIM-3 (Rangachari et al., 2012). TIGIT disrupted dimerisation of the costimulatory receptor CD226 on the same cell, and in mouse tumour and chronic-infection models combined TIGIT and PD-L1 antibody blockade enhanced CD8 T-cell function in a CD226-dependent way (Johnston et al., 2014). Staining for a checkpoint measures a component in sampled cells and not ligand contact or causal inhibition: PD-1-positive cells need not all be exhausted or cancer-reactive, more staining does not prove more inhibition or greater drug benefit, and TIM-3-positive cells do not select TIM-3 over PD-1 blockade. A checkpoint inhibitor interrupts one pathway: it does not teach T cells a new target, build a route into the tumour or repair every dysfunctional cell, and changing normal regulation can also harm healthy organs.

records.name: Cold tumours: immune deserts and exclusion
records.tldr: Sparse T cells and T cells gathered outside malignant regions are different immune patterns. An inflamed tumour can still restrain its T cells, and a pattern alone does not select a treatment.
records.summary:
Immune deserts have few relevant T cells in the sampled regions; immune exclusion describes cells nearby with limited entry into malignant nests. Deficient antigen availability or priming, recruitment signals, vascular interactions and stromal access can produce different distributions. Tumour WNT/beta-catenin-associated loss of dendritic-cell recruitment is one model-supported route to absent infiltration. An inflamed pattern can coexist with induced inhibitory signals, regulatory cells and exhausted programmes.

These are hypotheses about distinct dependencies. The same cancer can contain different regions or sites and can change with treatment. Matrix or cell abundance, a mixed RNA signature and spatial counts are different measurements. A proposed converter or HLA-independent recognition system still needs target, access, function, safety and comparative outcome evidence. There is no universal conversion treatment or hot/cold cutoff implied by the framework.

records.name: Immune exclusion
records.tldr: Immune exclusion describes immune cells concentrated outside cancer-cell regions. Their distribution raises questions about access; it does not identify the barrier or a treatment that will overcome it.
records.summary:

An excluded distribution records where cells were found. It does not establish why they stopped. A cell that has reached a target but is inhibited has a different measured problem, although access and functional failures can coexist.

Candidate mechanisms include recruitment signals, vascular interactions, matrix architecture, fibroblast signalling and myeloid-cell contacts. Their evidence comes from different cancers, human tissue studies and experimental models. A location measurement, causal perturbation and successful clinical intervention are different claims. Dense stroma alone does not diagnose exclusion or identify a safe way to reverse it.

Multiplex imaging can separately count CD8 cells in stroma and malignant nests and measure distances. Bulk chemokine, fibroblast or TGF-beta RNA programmes lose direct location. A high stromal TIL area score can therefore coexist with exclusion. In a fictional comparison, collagen-rich stroma with peripheral CD8 cells and high TGF-beta suggests a different access question from sparse T cells with low recruiting chemokines. Both remain hypotheses requiring appropriate measurements and functional controls, rather than diagnoses from one image.

Feig’s pancreatic mouse model found T cells outside cancer-cell regions coated with CAF-derived CXCL12; fibroblast depletion or CXCR4 blockade improved access and revealed checkpoint-antibody activity in that model. A common blood-borne effector route separates recruitment from vessel entry, movement through stroma and contact with relevant cancer cells. Rolling, firm adhesion and passage across vessel lining are distinct steps; in the melanoma transfer models, CXCR3 loss impaired firm arrest and extravasation without preventing initial rolling. A cell can inspect peptide-HLA on other cells along the way, so entering a cancer-cell nest is not the first possible recognition event.

Two fictional biopsies pose different access questions. A has CD8 cells in collagen-dense stroma, few in malignant nests and a high TGF-beta signature. B has few T cells and low CXCL9/CXCL10. Even a 40% stromal TIL score can coexist with few CD8 cells in nests, because eligible stromal area and intranest CD8 counts have different denominators.

records.name: Immune surveillance and cancer immunoediting
records.tldr: Immune responses can control cancer and select which populations persist. Immunoediting is a testable framework, not a way to assign a phase or recurrence risk from one scan.
records.summary:
The claim. Immune surveillance concerns recognition and control of transformed cells. Immunoediting adds selection of the populations that persist. Elimination, equilibrium and escape are conceptual processes that can coexist or occur independently. Their assignment requires evidence of control, restraint or outgrowth and its mechanism; they are not a compulsory calendar for every clinical cancer. The immune system therefore both protects against cancer and shapes the cancers that emerge.

Who and when. Ehrlich 1909; Burnet 1957 and 1970 and Thomas 1959 stated the surveillance hypothesis. Stutman's 1974 finding that athymic nude mice were no more prone to chemically induced tumours seemed to refute it. Shankaran, Old and Schreiber showed in 2001 that mice lacking lymphocytes or interferon-gamma signalling develop more tumours and that tumours from immunodeficient mice are more immunogenic, which is the signature of editing. Dunn and colleagues named immunoediting in 2002; Schreiber, Old and Smyth reviewed it in 2011. Allison's 1996 CTLA-4 blockade and Honjo's PD-1 discovery gave it its therapy; Chen and Mellman's cancer-immunity cycle (2013) is its clinical map.

Evidence for. Immunodeficient mice develop more spontaneous and induced tumours. Organ transplant recipients on immunosuppression have higher rates of many cancers, not only virus-driven ones. Immune-cell and outcome associations vary across cancers and measurements. Some tumour studies show neoantigen depletion or HLA loss consistent with editing, with other explanations and sampling limits still relevant. Checkpoint inhibitors produce durable remissions in melanoma, lung, kidney, bladder and mismatch repair-deficient cancers, while mutation count, candidate neoantigens or viral origin alone do not establish an individual response.

Evidence against and limits. Nude mice retain immune functions and are not a clean comparison of every immune mechanism; Shankaran also noted that they do not completely lack functional T cells. The episode illustrates the importance of the precise model. Most cancers arise in people with normal immunity, and the immune system also promotes cancer through inflammation. Equilibrium is difficult to observe directly in humans. Immunotherapy fails in most patients with pancreatic, prostate and brain cancers, and the reasons are only partly understood.

Predictions that held or failed. Held: releasing checkpoints unleashes anti-tumour immunity; particular studies find loss of recognised antigens under immune pressure; adoptive transfer of tumour-reactive T cells can cure. Failed: most therapeutic cancer vaccines of the 1990s and 2000s; the expectation that boosting immunity non-specifically (interferon, interleukin-2 in most settings) would be broadly effective.

Therapies that came from it. Checkpoint inhibitors (ipilimumab, nivolumab, pembrolizumab and successors), CAR-T cells, tumour-infiltrating lymphocyte therapy (lifileucel), T-cell engagers, neoantigen mRNA vaccines and the use of mutational burden and mismatch repair deficiency as predictive biomarkers. It applies clonal evolution to the immune system as predator, draws on the microenvironment view for the mechanisms of escape, and entered the hallmarks in 2011.

Status: model experiments and human observations support immune control and selection. They do not establish a universal sequence of phases, the fraction of all cancers prevented, or a personal recurrence forecast.

Elimination, equilibrium and escape describe processes that can coexist or occur independently, not a mandatory three-stage calendar. Shankaran’s genetically defined mouse experiments support lymphocyte and interferon-gamma contributions to control and selection. Recognition and comparable conditions are separate evidence; a larger share does not mean that pressure created more B cells. This example is distinct from 900/100 becoming 90/90, where B’s share rises while its count falls.

An editing claim combines longitudinal populations or antigens, recognition or functional assays and relevant comparisons. Apparent antigen loss can instead reflect sampling, detection limits, expression change or another treatment. Neither sequencing alone nor a killing experiment reconstructs the whole history. One immune-rich sample, negative blood test or model cannot assign an individual postoperative phase, explain every recurrence or forecast personal risk; different lesions can face different pressures.

Immune escape can involve loss of a targeted antigen, altered HLA alleles or processing, defective inducible signalling, inhibition after entry or impaired access. Anagnostou found loss of putative neoantigens in checkpoint-resistant lung tumours with accompanying T-cell evidence. McGranahan described allele-specific HLA loss in lung cancer evolution. Montesion’s commercial pan-cancer genomic series contained 83,644 samples with HLA-I loss of heterozygosity in 17%; this assay-defined pan-cancer observation is not a breast-specific prevalence. Allele loss differs from reversible expression change or a B2M defect affecting class-I surface display.

In Zaretsky’s selected four-person melanoma relapse series, two cases had JAK1 or JAK2 loss-of-function changes with loss of the normal allele and another had a truncating B2M change. The JAK2-deficient relapse cells failed to increase interferon-gamma signalling, PD-L1 and class I while retaining interferon-alfa/beta responsiveness. Engineered JAK1- or JAK2-deficient melanoma cells were still recognized by the tested NY-ESO-1-specific T cells. Baseline display, inducibility, recognition and killing are separate dependencies; neither a JAK variant nor detectable HLA alone answers all of them.

In a fictional controlled comparison, both cultures have baseline class I; only the control increases its signal and surface display after interferon gamma. The candidate retains an interferon-alfa response, and restoring JAK2 restores the tested gamma response. With matched handling, viability and restoration controls, this supports a model-specific JAK2-dependent inducibility defect. It is not proof of a particular displayed peptide, safe clinical rescue, tumour access or useful killing. JAK1 and JAK2 have different interferon dependencies.

Treatment can select a pre-existing population and new changes can arise. Earlier specimens, retained alleles, expression, stimulation and controlled functional comparisons help test an escape explanation. Different sites may have different bottlenecks; several mechanisms may coexist. Blood tumour DNA alone does not identify a particular escape route. A proposed HLA-independent recognizer or combination still needs its own target, access, function and safety evidence, and a restored laboratory endpoint does not establish clinical benefit.

records.name: Immune system
records.tldr: The body's defence network of cells and molecules that recognises and destroys infected, foreign and abnormal cells. It kills most would-be cancers before they are ever noticed; the ones that survive have learned to hide from it.
records.summary: Innate immunity uses inherited sensing systems (barriers, soluble defences such as complement, phagocytes such as macrophages and neutrophils, natural killer cells, and sensors of microbial or damage-related features), while adaptive immunity expands T cells and B cells whose diverse antigen receptors are assembled during development and selected by an encounter, with some descendants persisting as memory cells. The two cooperate: dendritic cells, cytokines and lymph nodes connect innate sensing to adaptive responses, and antibodies and T cells in turn guide innate cells.

notes: Fast and memoryless against slow and remembering is a starting tendency and not a rule: mice lacking functional T and B cells were protected against repeat Candida albicans infection in a monocyte-dependent way (Quintin et al., 2012), and natural killer cells carrying the Ly49H receptor expanded about 100-fold in the spleen after mouse cytomegalovirus infection, persisted for months and expanded again after transfer to a new host (Sun et al., 2009).

A list of cell types is a roster and not a functional report: a cell-family name does not show what a cell is doing, a marker shared by several populations is not a complete identity test (single-cell sequencing of human blood found six dendritic-cell and four monocyte subtypes; Villani et al., 2017), and a fraction of immune cells depends on its denominator (percent of recovered immune cells, of T cells and of all tissue cells are different quantities). Blood composition does not substitute for tumour composition, and a count of immune cells in a tumour does not by itself show recognition or killing. CD4 and CD8 are co-receptors and not permanent helper and killer assignments, tumour-associated macrophage names a setting, myeloid-derived suppressor cells need an operational phenotype and a test of suppressive function, and natural killer T cells are a T-cell family distinct from natural killer cells despite the name. In the classical description innate immunity is rapid and without immunologic memory while adaptive immunity is antigen-specific with a capacity for memory, and the two are not mutually exclusive (Marshall et al., 2018). Cytotoxic CD4 T cells have been found in infections, tumours and inflammatory disease, so a CD4 or CD8 label does not fix a helper or killer role (Venkatesh et al., 2023), and a myeloid-derived suppressor cell label rests on myeloid origin plus shown suppressive function (Bronte et al., 2016). CD4 and CD8 are coreceptors for T-cell receptors that recognise MHC, and a review discusses how they help impose MHC specificity during thymic selection (Van Laethem et al., 2012), so a CD4 or CD8 label names a coreceptor and not a job.

Among innate cells, phagocytes (neutrophils and macrophages) engulf and kill microbes, and natural killer cells play a major role in the rejection of tumours and the destruction of virus-infected cells through perforins and granzymes (Marshall et al., 2018). The receptor comparison concerns how recognition equipment is generated: inherited, germline-encoded receptors include Toll-like and natural killer receptors, whereas developing T and B cells assemble diverse antigen receptors by somatic V(D)J recombination (Hayday and Vantourout, 2020; Oettinger et al., 1990; Nemazee, 2017); one review describes the adaptive system as in turn activating innate effector mechanisms in an antigen-specific manner (Medzhitov, 2007).

Most adjuvants are thought to enhance T-cell and B-cell responses by engaging the innate immune system and not the lymphocytes directly (Coffman et al., 2010), so a vaccine can create an inflammatory context, and a response to an unrelated control antigen has to be measured to show that a response to the vaccine antigen is selective; in OnCo's reasoning, a manufactured antibody is also not evidence that the recipient made antibodies. Counts of cells, concentrations in picograms per millilitre and antigen-matched functional assays answer different questions, and a report should say which specimen, which time, which stimulation and which background control was used (OnCo reporting advice).

Tumours are recognised because they display mutated proteins and stress signals, but successful tumours evade destruction by displaying 'don't attack me' checkpoint signals, hiding their antigens, recruiting suppressive cells, and walling themselves off; 'avoiding immune destruction' is one of the hallmarks of cancer. Immunotherapy in its many forms (checkpoint inhibitors, engineered T cells, bispecifics, vaccines) aims to restore or engineer the immune system's ability to see and kill the tumour.

Cell-family roster, T cells: diverse antigen receptors support antigen-specific responses; functions can include help through signals, regulation and target-cell killing. A CD4 or CD8 marker is a coreceptor label, not a permanent helper or killer assignment. Interpretation: the presence of T cells does not establish which antigen they recognise or that killing is occurring (Marshall et al., 2018; Venkatesh et al., 2023).

Cell-family roster, B cells and plasma cells: B cells recognise antigen, can present it to T cells and can produce cytokine signals; plasma cells specialise in antibody secretion (Marshall et al., 2018; de Gruijter et al., 2022). Interpretation: counting either family does not identify what its antibodies bind or whether those antibodies help control a tumour.

Cell-family roster, natural killer cells: activating and inhibitory inputs together influence target-cell damage and cytokine production; these cells can release perforin, granzymes and interferon gamma (Marshall et al., 2018). Interpretation: a count of natural killer cells does not show that every abnormal cell will be attacked. The required signals, cell state and tested target still matter.

Cell-family roster, macrophages: engulfment, antigen presentation and signalling coexist with roles in tissue maintenance and repair. The repair, inflammatory and fibrotic programmes described by Wynn and Vannella (2016) depend on context. Interpretation: a macrophage count or location does not establish a universally beneficial or suppressive function.

Cell-family roster, dendritic cells: they collect and display antigen and provide signals that can shape T-cell priming, connecting innate and adaptive immunity (Marshall et al., 2018). Interpretation: their presence does not establish that the relevant antigen was displayed with the supporting signals needed for a useful response.

Cell-family roster, neutrophils: engulfment and antimicrobial activity are accompanied by inflammatory signalling and tissue effects. Afonso et al. (2012) showed cell-to-cell signal relay by leukotriene B4 in defined neutrophil chemotaxis experiments, including cells from mice with or without the formyl peptide receptor 1. Peiseler and Kubes (2019) review roles in tissue damage, resolution of inflammation and repair, including sterile injury. Interpretation: a neutrophil count alone does not diagnose infection or establish cancer promotion or cancer control.

Recognition-system comparison: innate recognition equipment is inherited; T-cell and B-cell antigen receptors are diversified and assembled during development. Exposure can change innate activation, recruitment and later responsiveness, while an adaptive response can select clones that expand, differentiate and persist as memory. Speed is a separate axis: innate responses are often early but can persist, and adaptive recall can be rapid. Mouse fungal and viral experiments demonstrate particular forms of trained monocyte or memory-like natural killer responses, not a rule that every innate response has conventional T-cell or B-cell memory (Quintin et al., 2012; Sun et al., 2009; Hayday and Vantourout, 2020). Antigen specificity alone does not establish activation or benefit.

Measurement comparison: cell counts describe a sampled population, protein concentration describes an amount per volume, and an antigen-matched functional assay describes an activity under its test conditions. Rodero et al. (2017) measured interferon-alpha protein, interferon-responsive RNA and antiviral activity as different readouts; Sanz et al. (2023) separately measured gamma-delta cell phenotype, receptor repertoire and target-cell killing. The reporting inference is to keep specimen, collection time, cell identity, stimulation, viability and background controls explicit. A concentration in picograms per millilitre is not a cell count or an antigen-specific response.

records.name: Interferon types I, II and III
records.tldr: Interferons are signalling proteins that change how cells respond to infection, stress and immune activity. There are three families with different receptors, and a short exposure, a long exposure and a missing response can each mean something different for a tumour.
records.summary: Type I interferons (alpha and beta) share a receptor system found on many cell types. Type II (gamma) uses a different receptor system and is made mainly by activated immune cells. The type I receptor, IFNAR, is expressed on virtually all nucleated cells and the type III receptor mainly on epithelial cells (Lazear et al., 2019), and interferon gamma production is largely restricted to immune cells although its receptor is widely expressed (Schneider et al., 2014). Interferon gamma effects include upregulated antigen processing and presentation and an antiviral state (Schroder et al., 2004). Type III (lambda) signals through a distinct receptor complex, made of IFN-lambda receptor 1 and IL-10 receptor 2, that signals through the Jak-STAT pathway (Kotenko et al., 2003); in mice the response to lambda was prominent in stomach, intestine and lung, very low in the brain and spleen, and restricted to epithelial cells in kidney and brain (Sommereyns et al., 2008). Types I, II and III group interferons by receptor usage; the alpha, beta, gamma and lambda names do not measure dose or potency. Many responses run through JAK and STAT proteins and can increase antigen-processing and HLA machinery, antiviral defences, or regulatory signals; producing an interferon, receiving it and carrying out a function are separate steps.

notes: In cancer, timing and the receiving cell decide the meaning. In mice, endogenous type I interferon was required to prevent the growth of carcinogen-induced and transplanted tumours, and the critical targets were host blood-lineage cells, not the tumour cells, which differs from interferon gamma, where tumour cells are important targets (Dunn et al., 2005). Prolonged interferon signalling in experimental tumours, driven by type II and maintained by types I and II, produced a resistance programme to checkpoint blockade that was PD-L1-dependent and independent, and biomarkers of that programme associated with progression after anti-PD-1 therapy in the patient data analysed (Benci et al., 2016). In four people with metastatic melanoma whose tumours first responded to pembrolizumab and later relapsed, paired biopsies showed loss-of-function mutations in JAK1 or JAK2 in two (with no response to interferon gamma in the mutant cells) and a truncating mutation in B2M, which removes class I display, in a third (Zaretsky et al., 2016). Four patients do not give a frequency for any cancer.

Reading an interferon result needs the family, the receiver, the timing and the readout. An interferon signature in RNA is not an interferon concentration and cannot identify the producing cell. Capacity to respond under a controlled exposure is not evidence of natural exposure, and an inducible display gene score is not a count of displayed peptide complexes or a measure of tumour killing. A working display pathway can also not repair a structural loss of an HLA allele or a processing component, and stronger or longer signalling is not safer or more beneficial by default. A report on an interferon experiment should name the family, the preparation, the concentration or units, the exposure time, the cell identity and viability, and the controls, and should keep three quantities apart: a concentration in picograms per millilitre, RNA expression, and a change from a matched unstimulated condition (OnCo reporting advice). A fourfold rise in a display-gene score is not fourfold killing.

Three measurement questions need separate answers. Protein concentration in a named fluid, for example picograms per millilitre, measures amount per volume. An RNA expression or signalling-protein readout measures a sampled cellular response. Change after controlled exposure relative to a matched unstimulated condition tests response capacity in that experiment. The last result does not establish that the same exposure occurred naturally, and a fluid concentration does not identify every producer or tissue exposure. Rodero et al. (2017) measured interferon-alpha protein, interferon-stimulated gene expression and antiviral activity separately; their activity assay measured protection from viral cytopathic effects, not tumour killing.

Ayers et al. (2017) studied an interferon-gamma-related tumour RNA profile associated with response to pembrolizumab. That expression score is not an interferon protein concentration or a count of killed cells, and an association among treated patients alone does not establish treatment benefit relative to no treatment. For a controlled-exposure result, report interferon family, preparation, concentration, exposure time, cell identity, viability and controls. A low baseline score can coexist with an inducible response; intact gene sequence alone does not establish working signalling. As a measurement inference, changing an expression score from 1 to 4 relative units is a fourfold change in that readout, not evidence of fourfold killing, peptide display or matching receptor recognition.

records.name: KEYNOTE-355
records.tldr: This trial found longer survival with pembrolizumab plus chemotherapy in its selected group with previously untreated advanced triple-negative breast cancer.
records.summary: KEYNOTE-355, trial NCT02819518 sponsored by Merck and published in the New England Journal of Medicine in 2022, established pembrolizumab plus chemotherapy as first-line treatment for metastatic triple-negative breast cancer with PD-L1 expression. It randomised 847 patients and met its primary progression-free and overall survival endpoints in tumours with a combined positive score of ten or more, in the prespecified CPS-ten-or-more comparison. This does not prove that the effect is exactly absent in every lower-score group. OnCo links it to triple-negative breast cancer, pembrolizumab, the CPS term, the TNBC roadmap and IMpassion131. Other first-line strategies, including ADC-based regimens, are separate comparisons; this trial alone cannot rank them.

The 2020 report stratified randomisation by previous exposure to the same chemotherapy class in neoadjuvant or adjuvant care. The later overall-survival report met its significance criterion for combined positive score ten or more; a nonsignificant broader subgroup or an untested significance comparison does not demonstrate exactly zero effect in each lower-score stratum.

The CPS-at-least-one analysis includes people with CPS at least ten. Its nonsignificant overall-survival comparison is therefore not an isolated result for CPS one to nine. Nested subgroup findings, the prespecified testing hierarchy and individual benefit are different questions; none establishes that every person below a cutoff has exactly zero treatment effect.

Grade 3 to 5 treatment-related adverse events 68.1 versus 66.9 percent.

UK access: NICE TA801 (29 June 2022) limits the regimen to CPS 10 or more with immune-cell staining below 1 percent, because atezolizumab with nab-paclitaxel (TA639) is commissioned for the immune-cell-positive group.

records.name: KEYNOTE-522
records.tldr: KEYNOTE-522 compared adding pembrolizumab before and after surgery with placebo on the same chemotherapy and surgery sequence in early triple-negative breast cancer. It measured improvements in response and survival.
records.summary: KEYNOTE-522 randomised 1,174 people with previously untreated stage II or III triple-negative breast cancer to a whole pembrolizumab or placebo strategy before and after surgery, with the same chemotherapy backbone. The first-602 pCR analysis reported 64.8% versus 51.2%. The 2022 report estimated three-year event-free survival at 84.5% versus 76.8%; the 2024 report estimated five-year overall survival at 86.6% versus 81.7%. An ASCO 2026 conference abstract reports seven-year EFS of 78.3% versus 69.8% and OS of 85.1% versus 77.2%. Keep each endpoint, analysis cohort and follow-up cutoff attached to its result. The trial did not separately randomise postoperative pembrolizumab or chemotherapy omission.

The preplanned exploratory residual-cancer-burden analysis (Annals of Oncology 2024) reported EFS hazard ratios for RCB-0, 1, 2 and 3 of 0.70 (95% confidence interval 0.38 to 1.31), 0.92 (0.39 to 2.20), 0.52 (0.32 to 0.82) and 1.24 (0.69 to 2.23). NICE TA851 (14 December 2022) commissions the regimen in England.
Label safety (Keytruda, 778 treated patients): serious adverse reactions 44 percent, fatal 0.9 percent, discontinuation of pembrolizumab 20 percent, most often for raised transaminases and rash.

The study question concerns the whole assigned sequence in previously untreated, non-metastatic stage II or III triple-negative breast cancer: T1c with N1 or N2, or T2 to T4 with N0 to N2, and performance status 0 or 1. The registry excludes prior checkpoint therapy and active autoimmune disease requiring systemic treatment in the preceding two years, among other criteria. There was one assignment of 784 people to pembrolizumab and 390 to placebo across preoperative chemotherapy, surgery and postoperative treatment, without a separate postoperative randomisation. Smaller node-negative tumours outside those entry criteria and metastatic disease are different settings. Entry did not require PD-L1 selection, and the high-risk early-stage indication in the prescribing information has no PD-L1 threshold.

The co-primary endpoints were pathological complete response at surgery, defined as ypT0/Tis ypN0, and event-free survival from randomisation. The response definition permits residual in-situ disease in the breast while excluding invasive residual cancer in breast and nodes. Event-free survival counts progression preventing definitive surgery, local or distant recurrence, a second primary cancer or death from any cause; overall survival is a secondary endpoint counting death from any cause. Because death is part of EFS, it is an event rather than a competing event for that composite. Analysing a recurrence component alone can require a different competing-risk question.

Keep the analysis cohorts separate. The 2020 first-interim pCR comparison used the first 602 randomised participants: 64.8% versus 51.2%, estimated difference 13.6 percentage points (95% confidence interval 5.4 to 21.8). The sponsor-posted first-1,002 comparison is 64.0% versus 54.7%, with a stratified difference of 9.2 points (2.8 to 15.6). That reported adjusted estimate is not simple subtraction of the rounded percentages. The current label also presents an all-1,174 pCR comparison, 63.0% versus 55.6%, estimated difference 7.5 points (1.6 to 13.4). These are different specified analysis populations, not interchangeable response claims.

At the fourth planned interim analysis reported in 2022, median follow-up was 39.1 months and all 1,174 participants contributed to the assigned-group survival comparison. Estimated 36-month EFS was 84.5% (95% confidence interval 81.7 to 86.9) versus 76.8% (72.2 to 80.7), with hazard ratio 0.63 (0.48 to 0.82). From the rounded survival estimates, the three-year absolute gain is 7.7 points, approximately eight additional people alive and event-free per 100, and number needed to treat is 1/0.077, about 13. The corresponding event risks are 15.5% versus 23.2%, a relative risk reduction of about 33%; the model's 37% lower hazard is a different measure.

The final overall-survival analysis published in 2024 used a March 22, 2024 cutoff and median follow-up of 75.1 months. Estimated 60-month OS was 86.6% versus 81.7%, with the paper reporting P=0.002; the label reports an OS hazard ratio of 0.66 (95% confidence interval 0.50 to 0.87) for the prespecified analysis. The absolute difference is 4.9 points, about five additional people alive per 100 at five years. Its reciprocal is 20.4, or 21 when rounding up to a whole-person number needed to treat. Neither this result nor the three-year EFS calculation identifies who benefits or combines benefit with harms. Comparing the 13.6-point pCR, 7.7-point EFS and 4.9-point OS gains does not show an effect shrinking over time: their endpoints, cohorts and horizons differ.

The ASCO 2026 conference abstract reports the later protocol-specified final follow-up, with an October 14, 2025 cutoff and median follow-up of 93.8 months. Seven-year EFS was 78.3% versus 69.8%, hazard ratio 0.68 (95% confidence interval 0.54 to 0.86); seven-year OS was 85.1% versus 77.2%, hazard ratio 0.64 (0.49 to 0.85). This is a conference abstract deposited by the authors, distinct from the 2024 full journal report and the sponsor-posted registry results. Longer observation of this cohort is not a second randomised trial.

Safety also retains its report and denominator. Across treatment phases, the 2020 paper reported treatment-related grade 3 or higher events in 78.0% versus 73.0%, including treatment-related deaths in 0.4% versus 0.3%. The label describes 778 versus 389 participants receiving at least one dose, distinct from the 784 versus 390 assigned. Its adverse-reaction categories and fatal-event figures must not be substituted for the paper's treatment-related categories. The prescribing information warns that immune-mediated reactions can arise after treatment stops and that hypothyroidism may require long-term hormone replacement. Event frequency, severity, duration, discontinuation and quality of life remain separate parts of the comparison.

The earlier adaptive phase 2 I-SPY2 report estimated pCR of 60% versus 22% in its triple-negative subgroup against its own chemotherapy control. That is a different comparison from KEYNOTE-522 and cannot establish a cross-trial treatment ranking. Likewise, better survival among people who achieve pCR is a prognostic association within selected response groups, not proof of the postoperative drug's separate effect or a validated rule selecting individual benefit. CTNeoBC found a strong pCR-outcome association but did not validate pCR as a trial-level surrogate for EFS or OS in its included trials. Here survival itself was measured.

The postoperative-only question remains distinct: OptimICE-pCR randomises people after pCR to postoperative pembrolizumab or observation, and the registry lists it as recruiting with no posted results. KEYNOTE-522 did not randomise dropping a chemotherapy component. CREATE-X compared postoperative capecitabine with standard postsurgical treatment after residual HER2-negative disease, while OlympiA compared olaparib with placebo in eligible high-risk germline BRCA1/2-associated HER2-negative disease after chemotherapy and local treatment. Those reports describe their own comparisons rather than a randomised test of adding either drug to the KEYNOTE-522 sequence. No result here is a personal forecast or a treatment-omission rule.

records.name: Ligand
records.tldr: A ligand binds a molecular partner. Binding does not necessarily activate a receptor or prove that a treatment will help.
records.summary: Hormones, growth factors and other molecules can bind receptors, but ligand describes the interaction rather than one functional effect. A bound ligand may activate a specified response, oppose another ligand, or show no effect in that assay. Some targeting ligands localize a payload. An accessible binding address need not be a cancer’s growth driver; delivery, intracellular action and clinical benefit require further evidence.

Estrogen and progesterone bind their distinct intracellular receptors, which can regulate transcription with different forms and cellular partners. FAP is a surface protease used as a targeting address, not a hormone/growth-factor receptor in this comparison.

Keep free versus added ligand, binding conditions, receptor accessibility, receiving cell, endpoint and time with the result. Surface staining, purified binding and living-cell response are separate assays. Growth dependence requires an appropriate functional perturbation; none of these observations alone establishes clinical eligibility.

In an invented comparison, a plain antibody binds surface protein A, the same binder carrying a payload damages tested cells, and a blocker lowers an internal signal. These establish different measured outcomes: accessible binding, activity of the finished construct, and an effect on the specified pathway. None alone establishes tumour dependence, healthy-tissue safety or patient benefit. Ask what binds what, what changes and which experiment measured the change; a shared address does not supply a shared action.

In another fictional experiment, opposing PD-1 binding to PD-L1 increases a stimulated T-cell response with receptor-specific controls. That does not make the antibody a PD-1 agonist: increased cell activity can follow antagonism of an inhibitory interaction. Name the receptor, receiving cell, assay and endpoint before interpreting whether a signal activates or restrains a response.

records.name: Lymph node
records.tldr: Small bean-shaped filters along the lymph vessels where immune cells gather. They are often the first place a cancer spreads, so surgeons check them to see how far the disease has gone.
records.summary: Lymph drains fluid from tissues back to the blood, passing through nodes where T and B cells inspect it for infection; cancer cells that enter lymph vessels lodge in the nearest nodes first, so node involvement (the N in TNM) is a central marker of a cancer's tendency to spread and raises the stage. Sentinel-node biopsy identifies and removes only the first node or two that drain a tumour, sparing patients the arm swelling (lymphoedema) that removing all nodes causes. Lymph nodes are also where immune responses against a tumour are launched, and where immunotherapy needs functioning T cells to be primed. Afferent vessels bring lymph into a node and efferent vessels carry it out, and a draining node names a route and not a finding of cancer. Immune material and cells reach a node by different routes: soluble antigen can reach resident dendritic cells through conduits in the node before migrating dendritic cells arrive (Sixt et al., 2005, mouse), while lymphocytes are recruited from the blood through high endothelial venules (Brulois et al., 2020, mouse). Lymph is interstitial fluid collected by lymph capillaries and returned to the venous blood (National Cancer Institute SEER training), so lymph and blood are different fluids and a sample of one does not stand in for the other. A tertiary lymphoid structure is an ectopic lymphoid aggregate that forms in tissue such as a tumour, and it is not a lymph node (Schumacher and Thommen, 2022). Size on imaging is a measurement in millimetres and not a finding of cancer or priming, and a report should say which node was measured, by what method and when (OnCo reporting advice). A node has a cortex, a paracortex and a medulla, and B cells and T cells home to separate areas within them (Willard-Mack, 2006); in the mouse, a venous population in the medulla was predicted to recruit myeloid cells rather than lymphocytes, which videomicroscopy confirmed (Brulois et al., 2020). In gene-targeted mice, loss of the chemokine receptor CCR7 altered the organisation of lymphoid organs and stopped skin dendritic cells reaching draining nodes (Förster et al., 1999). Arrival of material in a node does not show that priming succeeded. Pathological involvement means cancer was identified in examined tissue, which differs from a drainage route, enlargement or an imaging observation, and a negative sampled node does not certify the unsampled nodes (the National Cancer Institute notes that a false-negative biopsy gives a false sense of security about the extent of cancer).

records.name: Macrophage states beyond M1 and M2
records.tldr: What a macrophage is doing depends on where it came from, where it sits, and the signals and history it has had, so the two-box labels M1 and M2 describe a laboratory comparison and not every macrophage in a tissue. In a tumour, a macrophage's label does not on its own show what it is doing to the cancer or to T cells.
records.summary: A macrophage's lineage is its developmental origin; its state is a set of activity programmes at one time. A state label describes selected features and is not a complete biography. The M1 and M2 scheme grew from simplified experiments, with interferon gamma and microbial stimulation giving M1-like cells and interleukin-4 giving M2-like cells, and it is ambiguous unless the source, the stimulus and the markers are stated. A consensus framework asks authors to report the source of the macrophages, the activators used and a defined set of markers (Murray et al., 2014). When human macrophages were stimulated with diverse signals, 299 transcriptomes revealed a spectrum of activation states that extends the M1 and M2 model (Xue et al., 2014). In mice, tissue-resident macrophages had distinct enhancer landscapes beyond what developmental origin explained, and the local environment could reshape transplanted precursors and even reprogramme differentiated macrophages moved to a new environment (Lavin et al., 2014). Together these support diversity and plasticity without showing that any macrophage can be converted to any desired state.

notes: In a tumour, a tumour-associated macrophage is named for its location, and its state and tested functions are separate questions. A tumour can hold several programmes in different neighbourhoods or at different times. An expression cluster can suggest a repair, interferon or lipid-handling programme, which is a hypothesis; it does not establish that the cells suppress T cells, kill cancer cells or would respond to a macrophage-directed drug. One marker such as CD163 does not establish a universal suppressive state, a change in proportions between two biopsies does not show that the same cells changed state, and the plain statement that M1 is good and M2 is bad loses the tissue and experiment that give a response its meaning.

Macrophages are described with protein panels, flow cytometry and single-cell RNA, and the report needs the identification rules, tissue or culture source, stimulation, collection time and denominator, because a fraction of recovered macrophages is not cells per area of tissue. A function such as engulfment or the effect on stimulated T-cell proliferation needs its own test with viability and comparator controls.

records.name: Multiplex immunofluorescence
records.tldr: This approach measures several protein markers in a tissue section, in one or more imaging cycles. Image analysis then estimates cells, counts and distances under defined rules.
records.summary: Multiplex immunofluorescence measures selected protein-marker signals in a tissue section, using one or several imaging cycles. Cyclic methods build a high-plex image of one section by repeating staining, imaging and signal removal and then registering the cycles: t-CyCIF produced up to 60-plex images of formalin-fixed specimens and showed that antigenicity changes with cycle number (Lin and colleagues, 2018), and IBEX imaged more than 65 parameters in one section by iterative staining and chemical bleaching (Radtke and colleagues, 2020). A six-institution study of a six-plex PD-1 and PD-L1 panel, imaged with a locked-down image analysis algorithm, reported average intersite concordance of cell densities of R squared 0.75 in breast carcinoma and 0.72 in non-small cell lung cancer tissue microarrays (Taube and colleagues, 2021); that is reproducibility for one specified panel and workflow, not for multiplex immunofluorescence in general. A cell phenotype is a rule-based call from the measured panel, a density needs a stated denominator, and a distance needs a stated definition (cell centre or cell boundary).

Centre-to-centre distance includes the cell interiors, while boundary-to-boundary distance spans only the gap, so the two rulers give different numbers for the same pair. Proximity under either rule is not contact, recognition or killing.

records.name: Myeloid-derived suppressor cells (MDSCs)
records.tldr: These heterogeneous myeloid populations are characterised using phenotype, suppressive function and context. A marker or blood-cell count alone does not establish them.
records.summary: Myeloid-derived suppressor cells are research-defined populations with demonstrable immune-suppressive activity and appropriate myeloid characteristics. Monocytic, polymorphonuclear and early-stage groups require species- and preparation-specific interpretation. Their phenotype overlaps other myeloid cells; a suggestive phenotype without established function needs qualification.

notes: Myeloid-derived suppressor cells are heterogeneous myeloid populations described using phenotype, suppressive function and context. They are not a unique lineage or a permanent identity defined by one marker, and populations can include mature and immature cells. The Bronte standards distinguish monocytic, polymorphonuclear and early-stage groups and recommend MDSC-like terminology for cells with a suggestive phenotype but no established suppressive activity.

Human research panels include CD11b-positive, CD14-positive, low or absent HLA-DR, CD15-negative monocytic candidates, and CD14-negative cells with CD15 or CD66b for polymorphonuclear candidates. Mouse Ly6C/Ly6G panels are different. Morphology, additional markers, preparation and species remain necessary. Neither CD11b alone nor CD11b-positive/CD3-negative blood cells establish suppression. Condamine linked LOX-1 to molecular and functional features of the studied human cancer-associated polymorphonuclear population; it is not a universal marker of every subtype.

Proposed suppressive routes include altered amino-acid availability, reactive molecules and inhibitory signalling, with effects depending on the population and experiment. Enzyme abundance or an RNA program does not measure the entire effect. For a suppression experiment, document candidate-cell purity and viability, adequate stimulation of responding T cells, T cells without the candidate population, suitable myeloid comparators, ratios and incubation time. Lower proliferation or cytokine output can also follow failed stimulation or cell death. The Bronte standards emphasise titration and appropriate phenotype-matched controls.

Retain the tissue or blood compartment, species, isolation, gating, time and treatment. A fraction of recovered cells differs from an absolute blood concentration, and neither directly measures tissue burden. Gradient separation, freezing and sorting can change recovery or behaviour; the standards specifically warn of losses after freezing, especially in polymorphonuclear populations. A lower post-procedure count alone does not establish removal of suppressive activity or clinical benefit.

The reasoning sequence is sample and species, candidate phenotype, controlled function, then a claim bounded to that context. A marker result cannot skip the functional question. No generic MDSC count or assay supplies a universal clinical cutoff or predicts benefit from depletion; such treatment claims need their own comparisons.

records.name: Necrosis
records.tldr: Necrosis describes cell and tissue breakdown with loss of membrane integrity. The appearance alone does not identify its cause.
records.summary: Necrotic appearance can follow overwhelming injury or regulated death mechanisms. A late membrane-integrity measurement cannot reconstruct the preceding death sequence. Histology describes the sampled region; necrosis there does not establish the absence of viable tumour elsewhere, treatment success or a particular molecular pathway. Distinguish tissue appearance from a mechanism established by controlled perturbation and complementary readouts. Inflammation and antigen-specific adaptive immune protection are separate outcomes.

notes: Necrosis describes loss of membrane integrity and tissue breakdown, rather than one molecular route. Overwhelming injury, regulated mechanisms and late secondary necrosis after apoptosis with inadequate clearance can converge on membrane loss. Necrosis is broader than necroptosis.

RIPK3-dependent MLKL activation is an example regulated necrotic mechanism. Sun and colleagues used biochemical and cellular perturbations to establish MLKL downstream of RIP3; a necrotic region or membrane-impermeant dye alone cannot establish that pathway.

Histology describes the sampled region; viable tumour may remain elsewhere. A membrane-compromised fraction, qualitative tissue necrosis and method-defined necrotic area answer different questions. Handling, delayed fixation and late sampling affect interpretation, and no universal necrosis percentage identifies a death mechanism or proves treatment success. Preparing and staining a section consumes tissue, while live-cell dye assays use tested aliquots and report a defined membrane-compromised fraction. Clinical morphology and experimental pathway perturbation have different validation contexts.

HMGB1-deficient necrotic cells produced less inflammation in defined experiments. That result concerns danger signalling, rather than automatic adaptive immune memory. Dye entry after an intervention cannot establish necroptosis, vaccine activity or clinical benefit without the separate causal and host tests.

records.name: Neoantigen
records.tldr: A peptide arising from altered tumour sequence can be an immune target if it is displayed and recognised. Prediction alone does not show safe tumour killing.
records.summary:
A tumour sequence change can produce a new peptide sequence, but the altered sequence, its expression, HLA presentation and T-cell recognition are separate findings. Candidate sources include substitutions, frameshifts, fusions and altered RNA joins; a workflow that assessed one class has not necessarily assessed the others.

Computational ranking can consider binding, expression and clonality. In the TESLA study, Wells and colleagues combined tumour-normal exomes, tumour RNA and HLA typing, then tested selected peptides for HLA binding and recognition by existing patient-matched T cells. The study focused on small somatic variants and class I antigens; it did not validate every fusion or splice source, every new response a vaccine might induce, or clinical benefit from a vaccine. A candidate peptide and a favourable prediction do not establish safe recognition of naturally presenting tumour cells.

notes: Once the recognition mechanism is clear, a candidate source list precedes HLA matching, target selection and product construction. Confirm alteration identity, tumour specificity and biological support first. DNA, RNA and protein answer different questions, and a longer list can add uncertain calls as well as genuine candidates. A DNA alteration can nominate a possible sequence without establishing the processed peptide that a conventional T cell will recognise.

For tumour DNA, retain local usable coverage, artefacts, tumour fraction and copy number with the call. For matched normal DNA, absence is conditional on suitable sampling, coverage and detection limits. Tumour RNA can support an altered transcript, but comes from a mixture of cells and depends on expression depth and processing. Protein or peptide detection is a further observation with its own method coverage, cell-of-origin question and detection limits; none of these measurements can simply stand in for the others.

A cancer-cell fraction estimate describes the sampled cancer cells, whereas truncal describes ancestry shared across sampled branches; a subclonal alteration belongs to a subset. One small biopsy need not establish the distribution across every site. Read fraction and ancestry do not show that a peptide is displayed, and an unobserved region or insufficiently sampled alteration remains a gap rather than a demonstrated negative.

In an invented comparison, candidate A has a supported tumour DNA alteration, no support in adequately assessed normal DNA and observed mutant RNA. It has progressed further as a source candidate, but processing, HLA display and T-cell recognition remain untested. Candidate B has tumour DNA support but inadequate normal coverage, so tumour specificity is still unresolved. These are evidence questions, not a numerical ranking algorithm.

Two more fictional candidates illustrate bounded negatives. Candidate C has only a weakly supported RNA junction and needs reproducibility and artefact checks. Candidate D has strong DNA support but no RNA detection in a shallow assay, which cannot establish that the transcript is absent. None of A to D has demonstrated HLA presentation or T-cell recognition merely from these starting observations.

Prepared specimens and analysis can introduce misleading candidates through fixation damage, contamination, misalignment or uncertain junctions. The chosen reference transcript also matters when translating an altered sequence. Preserve specimen identity, coordinates and alleles, transcript/reference, method and software versions, usable coverage, thresholds and manual decisions so the result can be traced to its source. A filter or annotation is not independent proof of function.

Parkhurst and colleagues found neoantigen-reactive cultured lymphocyte populations in 62 of 75 people with gastrointestinal cancers. About 1.6% of the tested protein-changing mutant gene products were recognised, and 99% of the recognised determinants were unique to one person. This is a selected study and assay result, not the probability that any mutation is processed, displayed or useful in breast cancer. Applying 0.016 to 60 fictional candidate mutations gives 0.96, about one, as an arithmetic illustration only.

In a fictional comparison, the same expressed mutation produces a nine-amino-acid peptide that is displayed by person A's HLA-A*02:01 and meets a matching receptor. Person B's tested classical class-I variants bind no mutation-spanning peptide adequately; a possible class-II response is a different question. If A's tumour later loses the required HLA allele, the mutation can remain while that recognition route fails. Several candidates sharing that allele do not provide independent protection. Tumour-specific sequence also does not guarantee that its receptor avoids unrelated healthy-tissue targets.

records.name: PD-L1 combined positive score 10 in triple-negative breast cancer
records.tldr: In metastatic triple-negative breast cancer the immunotherapy pembrolizumab is only given when a PD-L1 stain of the tumour scores 10 or more on the combined positive score, because that is the group in which the trial showed people lived longer. For early disease before surgery no PD-L1 test is needed: pembrolizumab helped regardless.
records.summary: The combined positive score is the number of PD-L1-staining tumour cells, lymphocytes and macrophages divided by the total number of viable tumour cells, multiplied by 100 (Cortes 2022). KEYNOTE-355 randomised 847 patients with untreated locally recurrent inoperable or metastatic triple-negative breast cancer 2:1 to pembrolizumab or placebo with the investigator's chemotherapy (nab-paclitaxel, paclitaxel or gemcitabine-carboplatin), with PD-L1 tested centrally by the 22C3 assay. Progression-free survival at the interim analysis was 9.7 against 5.6 months in the CPS 10 or more group (hazard ratio 0.65, primary objective met), 7.6 against 5.6 months in CPS 1 or more (0.74, not significant) and 7.5 against 5.6 months overall (0.82, not tested), the effect increasing with PD-L1 enrichment (Cortes 2020). At the final analysis (median follow-up 44.1 months) overall survival in the CPS 10 group was 23.0 against 16.1 months (hazard ratio 0.73, significant), 17.6 against 16.0 months in CPS 1 or more (0.86, not significant) and 17.2 against 15.5 months in all patients (0.89, not tested); grade 3 to 5 treatment-related events occurred in 68.1 against 66.9 percent (Cortes 2022). NICE recommends pembrolizumab with paclitaxel or nab-paclitaxel for untreated triple-negative locally recurrent unresectable or metastatic breast cancer in the population the appraisal covers (TA801, June 2022). A different assay and score defined the earlier atezolizumab result: IMpassion130 used the SP142 immune-cell score with positivity at 1 percent or more of the tumour area; median progression-free survival was 7.5 against 5.0 months and overall survival 25.0 against 15.5 months in the PD-L1-positive subgroup, without a significant overall survival gain in the whole population (Schmid 2018), and the parent page's history records that approval was later withdrawn. Early disease needs no PD-L1 test: in KEYNOTE-522 pembrolizumab with chemotherapy raised pathological complete response from 51.2 to 64.8 percent in stage II and III disease unselected for PD-L1 (Schmid 2020) and five-year overall survival from 81.7 to 86.6 percent (Schmid 2024); NICE TA851 (December 2022) recommends it for triple-negative early or locally advanced breast cancer at high risk of recurrence. The biomarker readout pd-l1-cps carries the label wording for every CPS threshold across cancers.

records.name: Protein
records.tldr: Proteins are amino-acid products that provide structure, catalysis, transport and signaling. A detected fragment and a complete working protein are different findings.
records.summary: Amino acids join through peptide bonds into polypeptide chains; linked amino acids are residues. Peptide and protein usage overlaps without a universal length boundary. A protein may contain one or several chains, folded domains and flexible regions. Processing, chemical modifications, localization, production and degradation affect its form and behavior. Genes specify coding templates, but a DNA or RNA finding does not measure the resulting protein’s intact structure or activity.
